skills.when_to_use_negative: The task is single-slice/2D image synthesis or the inputs are not co-registered volumetric MRI/PRI pairs at ~256^3 resolution — the 3D GAN's benefit is volumetric consistency Computational resources are limited: SC-GAN requires lengthy training and heavy GPU memory, so a 3D Unet or 2D network may be the practical choice The target is a quantitative modality whose absolute values matter (e.g., DTI metrics) and min-max rescaling to 0-1 would distort the quantitative values — the authors advise avoiding the normalization step for such targets

skills.search_text: admm-constrained-optimization-execution Use when a time-optimal MRI gradient waveform must be generated on-the-fly from a flexible set of input constraints (moments, eddy currents, PNS, b-value, duty cycle) using GrOpt's ADMM solver. The problem requires optimizing readout trajectories or slice-select gradients, which the GrOpt toolbox has not been used to optimize A proof of convexity is required for the multi-constraint solution space, which is difficult to establish Concomitant field terms, acoustic noise, or gradient heating limits must be constrained — these are future work and not yet included in the toolbox http://edamontology.org/topic_3300 http://edamontology.org/topic_3444 Execute GrOpt's ADMM-based constrained optimizer (C kernels wrapped in Cython/Python or Matlab) to solve MRI gradient waveform design problems defined by hardware limits (Gmax, Smax), raster time dt, and modular constraints such as gradient moment nulling, eddy-current nulling, and PNS limits. proteomics/v1 10.1002/mrm.28384

skills.search_text: admm-solver-configuration Use when you need to solve a constrained MRI gradient waveform design problem — e.g. gmax, smax, gradient moment nulling, eddy current or PNS constraints — via GrOpt's ADMM solver and need correct stopping, tolerance, and warm-start configuration. The task is optimizing readout trajectories or slice-select gradients — the article states the GrOpt toolbox has not been used to optimize readout trajectories or slice-select gradients You need constraints not yet in GrOpt, such as concomitant field terms, acoustic noise, or gradient heating limits — these are listed as future work Very long waveforms (e.g. multiecho turbo-spin echo), where the default choice of N and dt may need adjustment http://edamontology.org/topic_3300 http://edamontology.org/topic_3444 Configure and run GrOpt's ADMM-based feasibility solver (implemented in C, wrapped with Cython for Python) to find gradient waveforms satisfying hardware and moment constraints, with the 20,000-iteration stopping rule and tolerance-based feasibility checks on ci(g) - ti bounds. proteomics/v1 10.1002/mrm.28384
skills.summary: Configure and run GrOpt's ADMM-based feasibility solver (implemented in C, wrapped with Cython for Python) to find gradient waveforms satisfying hardware and moment constraints, with the 20,000-iteration stopping rule and tolerance-based feasibility checks on ci(g) - ti bounds.

skills.description: Use when training a 3D conditional GAN for cross-modality image synthesis (e.g. T1w+FLAIR MRI to amyloid PET) shows unstable or non-converging adversarial optimization, and you need spectral normalization/feature-matching stabilization.
skills.name: adversarial-training-stabilization-techniques
skills.search_text: adversarial-training-stabilization-techniques Use when training a 3D conditional GAN for cross-modality image synthesis (e.g. T1w+FLAIR MRI to amyloid PET) shows unstable or non-converging adversarial optimization, and you need spectral normalization/feature-matching stabilization. Input task has no adversarial component (e.g. a plain 3D Unet regression) — spectral normalization and feature matching specifically target GAN training stabilization and do not apply. GPU memory or training time is severely constrained — the paper notes computational cost is the main limitation of SC-GAN, requiring lengthy training and heavy GPU memory. You only need image preprocessing/registration (N4ITK correction, ANTs coregistration, FSL TOPUP/EDDY) — this skill concerns GAN training stabilization, not upstream data preparation. http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 http://edamontology.org/topic_3306 Stabilizes training of a 3D conditional GAN (SC-GAN) for multimodal neuroimaging synthesis by combining spectral normalization, a feature matching loss, and a modified loss function (L1 + brain-area RMSE), so the generator-discriminator optimization converges for 256x256x256 MRI/PET inputs. proteomics/v1 10.1002/mrm.28819
skills.summary: Stabilizes training of a 3D conditional GAN (SC-GAN) for multimodal neuroimaging synthesis by combining spectral normalization, a feature matching loss, and a modified loss function (L1 + brain-area RMSE), so the generator-discriminator optimization converges for 256x256x256 MRI/PET inputs.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input task has no adversarial component (e.g. a plain 3D Unet regression) — spectral normalization and feature matching specifically target GAN training stabilization and do not apply. GPU memory or training time is severely constrained — the paper notes computational cost is the main limitation of SC-GAN, requiring lengthy training and heavy GPU memory. You only need image preprocessing/registration (N4ITK correction, ANTs coregistration, FSL TOPUP/EDDY) — this skill concerns GAN training stabilization, not upstream data preparation.

skills.description: Use when you have a MUSCLE multiple sequence alignment of protein variants and need per-position absolute and relative amino acid occurrence tables, or a consensus sequence with user-defined conservation thresholding.
skills.name: amino-acid-frequency-matrix-construction
skills.search_text: amino-acid-frequency-matrix-construction Use when you have a MUSCLE multiple sequence alignment of protein variants and need per-position absolute and relative amino acid occurrence tables, or a consensus sequence with user-defined conservation thresholding. The goal is SNP-level variant reporting (frequency, variants, type of variant per position) rather than amino acid occurrence matrices — scop3D's SNP variants analysis produces a different matrix annotating the protein sequence with SNP frequency and type. You need conservation mapped onto a 3D structure (percentage conservation or information entropy in PDB B-values) — that is the downstream structure-annotation part, which consumes these matrices rather than producing them. http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Builds two per-position matrices from a multiple sequence alignment: one annotating the consensus sequence with the absolute abundance of each amino acid per position, and one converting those counts into relative abundances in percent. This is the scop3D sequence-conservation reporting step that yields the text-file outputs backing the tool's 3D conservation visualization. proteomics/v1 10.1002/pmic.201400354
skills.summary: Builds two per-position matrices from a multiple sequence alignment: one annotating the consensus sequence with the absolute abundance of each amino acid per position, and one converting those counts into relative abundances in percent. This is the scop3D sequence-conservation reporting step that yields the text-file outputs backing the tool's 3D conservation visualization.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is SNP-level variant reporting (frequency, variants, type of variant per position) rather than amino acid occurrence matrices — scop3D's SNP variants analysis produces a different matrix annotating the protein sequence with SNP frequency and type. You need conservation mapped onto a 3D structure (percentage conservation or information entropy in PDB B-values) — that is the downstream structure-annotation part, which consumes these matrices rather than producing them.

skills.description: Use when you have FT-ICR MS molecular formula lists (element composition with C/H/O/N/P/S) and need aromaticity classification or DBE-based traits for dissolved organic matter molecules.
skills.name: aromaticity-index-computation
skills.search_text: aromaticity-index-computation Use when you have FT-ICR MS molecular formula lists (element composition with C/H/O/N/P/S) and need aromaticity classification or DBE-based traits for dissolved organic matter molecules. Input is raw FT-ICR MS spectra or peaks without assigned molecular formulas — traits cannot be computed on uncharacterized 'dark matter' molecules The goal is molecular class assignment, chemical diversity/dissimilarity, or DOM-microbe network analyses (commProc, iDME, H2, iCER) — these are separate iDOM functions, not molTrait The dataset is not molecular compositional DOM data (e.g. taxonomic abundance tables) http://edamontology.org/topic_0102 Computes the modified aromaticity index (AImod) and double-bond-equivalent traits (DBE, DBEO, DBEAI) from DOM molecular formulas as part of iDOM's molTrait function, turning FT-ICR MS molecular compositional data into chemical characteristic descriptors. proteomics/v1 10.1002/mlf2.70002
skills.summary: Computes the modified aromaticity index (AImod) and double-bond-equivalent traits (DBE, DBEO, DBEAI) from DOM molecular formulas as part of iDOM's molTrait function, turning FT-ICR MS molecular compositional data into chemical characteristic descriptors.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw FT-ICR MS spectra or peaks without assigned molecular formulas — traits cannot be computed on uncharacterized 'dark matter' molecules The goal is molecular class assignment, chemical diversity/dissimilarity, or DOM-microbe network analyses (commProc, iDME, H2, iCER) — these are separate iDOM functions, not molTrait The dataset is not molecular compositional DOM data (e.g. taxonomic abundance tables)

skills.name: asa-benchmark-validation-against-reference
skills.search_text: asa-benchmark-validation-against-reference Use when you have reimplemented or modified a solvent-exposure calculation (water molecules in possible contact per residue) and need to prove numerical correctness against published reference ASA values. The goal is secondary structure assignment, not solvent exposure — DSSP does not predict secondary structure, and ASA validation is unrelated to hydrogen-bond pattern recognition (turns, bridges, helices, ladders) The structure already carries annotated ASA values in a trusted DSSP entry from the Protein Data Bank, so recomputation and benchmarking are unnecessary You need dynamic/time-averaged solvent exposure from an ensemble or MD trajectory; this skill validates static ASA from a single set of atomic coordinates http://edamontology.org/topic_0081 Validates a geodesic-sphere solvent-accessible-surface-area (ASA) implementation by comparing per-residue areas against the published Lee and Richards values for myoglobin, using graded tolerances tied to test-point density (<=4 A^2 at 80 points, <=1 A^2 at 320 points). proteomics/v1 10.1002/bip.360221211
skills.summary: Validates a geodesic-sphere solvent-accessible-surface-area (ASA) implementation by comparing per-residue areas against the published Lee and Richards values for myoglobin, using graded tolerances tied to test-point density (<=4 A^2 at 80 points, <=1 A^2 at 320 points).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is secondary structure assignment, not solvent exposure — DSSP does not predict secondary structure, and ASA validation is unrelated to hydrogen-bond pattern recognition (turns, bridges, helices, ladders) The structure already carries annotated ASA values in a trusted DSSP entry from the Protein Data Bank, so recomputation and benchmarking are unnecessary You need dynamic/time-averaged solvent exposure from an ensemble or MD trajectory; this skill validates static ASA from a single set of atomic coordinates

skills.description: Use when you have a muSignAl output table of candidate signatures (e.g. sign_cvd2.xlsx) with per-signature AUC values and need to select the high-performing subset above a specified AUC threshold such as 0.95.
skills.name: auc-based-signature-performance-thresholding
skills.search_text: auc-based-signature-performance-thresholding Use when you have a muSignAl output table of candidate signatures (e.g. sign_cvd2.xlsx) with per-signature AUC values and need to select the high-performing subset above a specified AUC threshold such as 0.95. Input is raw proteomic or omic intensity data (e.g. AD.xlsx) rather than an already-generated muSignAl signature output file — run the muSignAl algorithm first. The goal is to discover new signatures rather than to rank/filter existing ones; use the muSignAl algorithm itself instead of this thresholding step. Signatures lack AUC values computed with pROC from glmnet-fitted models, so the threshold cannot be applied meaningfully. http://edamontology.org/topic_3577 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Filters multi-omic signatures produced by muSignAl by predictive performance, keeping only those whose AUC (computed with pROC from glmnet-fitted models) exceeds a fixed cutoff (e.g. AUC > 0.95), reproducing the paper's Table 1 selection of 47 of 158 signatures on the Olink CVD-II dataset. proteomics/v1 10.1002/pmic.202200252
skills.summary: Filters multi-omic signatures produced by muSignAl by predictive performance, keeping only those whose AUC (computed with pROC from glmnet-fitted models) exceeds a fixed cutoff (e.g. AUC > 0.95), reproducing the paper's Table 1 selection of 47 of 158 signatures on the Olink CVD-II dataset.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw proteomic or omic intensity data (e.g. AD.xlsx) rather than an already-generated muSignAl signature output file — run the muSignAl algorithm first. The goal is to discover new signatures rather than to rank/filter existing ones; use the muSignAl algorithm itself instead of this thresholding step. Signatures lack AUC values computed with pROC from glmnet-fitted models, so the threshold cannot be applied meaningfully.

skills.search_text: auc-model-evaluation Use when repeated subsample models (e.g. Elastic Net glmnet fits) must be scored for predictive performance and filtered on AUC > 0.5 before downstream feature selection. When the input is already a validated feature/signature table rather than fitted subsample models — the AUC filter only makes sense per fitted model, not per feature. When the goal is to select signatures without measuring predictive performance — muSignAl's selection is explicitly tied to 'multiple signatures with similar predictive performance', so an AUC evaluation stage is mandatory in this workflow. http://edamontology.org/topic_3577 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Evaluates predictive models built within the muSignAl workflow by computing the area under the ROC curve (AUC) with pROC, and retains only models whose AUC exceeds 0.5 so that feature importance is computed from predictive (better-than-random) subsample models. proteomics/v1 10.1002/pmic.202200252
skills.summary: Evaluates predictive models built within the muSignAl workflow by computing the area under the ROC curve (AUC) with pROC, and retains only models whose AUC exceeds 0.5 so that feature importance is computed from predictive (better-than-random) subsample models.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the input is already a validated feature/signature table rather than fitted subsample models — the AUC filter only makes sense per fitted model, not per feature. When the goal is to select signatures without measuring predictive performance — muSignAl's selection is explicitly tied to 'multiple signatures with similar predictive performance', so an AUC evaluation stage is mandatory in this workflow.

skills.description: Use when you have X-ray protein structures in PDB format (ATOMIC ATOM records with Cα B-factors) and need normalized B'-factor/ΔB' profiles or mobility-based (rigidification vs. flexibility gain) interpretation at ligand-binding sites.
skills.name: b-factor-profile-normalization
skills.search_text: b-factor-profile-normalization Use when you have X-ray protein structures in PDB format (ATOMIC ATOM records with Cα B-factors) and need normalized B'-factor/ΔB' profiles or mobility-based (rigidification vs. flexibility gain) interpretation at ligand-binding sites. Input structures are not X-ray structures or lack per-residue B-factors (e.g. NMR ensembles or predicted models), since the method normalizes X-ray B-factor profiles You need quantitative thermodynamic or kinetic mobility measurements rather than a crystallographic B'-factor/ΔB' interpretation http://edamontology.org/topic_0102 Normalizes raw per-residue B-factors from X-ray PDB structures into B' profiles and computes per-residue ΔB' deviations using the BANΔIT JavaScript browser toolkit, because protein mobility changes have been associated with protein-ligand interaction quality and structure-based drug design. proteomics/v1 10.1002/minf.202000144
skills.summary: Normalizes raw per-residue B-factors from X-ray PDB structures into B' profiles and computes per-residue ΔB' deviations using the BANΔIT JavaScript browser toolkit, because protein mobility changes have been associated with protein-ligand interaction quality and structure-based drug design.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input structures are not X-ray structures or lack per-residue B-factors (e.g. NMR ensembles or predicted models), since the method normalizes X-ray B-factor profiles You need quantitative thermodynamic or kinetic mobility measurements rather than a crystallographic B'-factor/ΔB' interpretation

skills.search_text: betanti-null-model-computation Use when FT-ICR MS-derived DOM molecular compositional data (e.g. MCD, TD, or TWCD molecular dendrograms) must be tested for deterministic versus stochastic assembly via betaNTI null modeling. Input is raw FT-ICR MS peak lists not yet converted to molecular compositional data or trait-based dendrograms — molecular class assignment and trait calculation must precede betaNTI null modeling The goal is quantifying dark matter effects on DOM interactions (use iDME) or DOM-microbe network specialization (use H2) rather than assembly processes http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Computes dendrogram-based beta nearest taxon index (betaNTI) values for dissolved organic matter (DOM) assemblages using the commProc function of the iDOM R package, quantifying whether deterministic or stochastic processes govern molecular assembly of FT-ICR MS-characterized DOM. proteomics/v1 10.1002/mlf2.70002
skills.summary: Computes dendrogram-based beta nearest taxon index (betaNTI) values for dissolved organic matter (DOM) assemblages using the commProc function of the iDOM R package, quantifying whether deterministic or stochastic processes govern molecular assembly of FT-ICR MS-characterized DOM.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw FT-ICR MS peak lists not yet converted to molecular compositional data or trait-based dendrograms — molecular class assignment and trait calculation must precede betaNTI null modeling The goal is quantifying dark matter effects on DOM interactions (use iDME) or DOM-microbe network specialization (use H2) rather than assembly processes

skills.description: Use when raw protein sequences in FASTA format must be converted into dense numerical embeddings for a machine-learning classifier (e.g. identifying plant R proteins with LGBM), and pretrained deep representation learning models are available.
skills.name: bidirectional-lstm-feature-extraction
skills.search_text: bidirectional-lstm-feature-extraction Use when raw protein sequences in FASTA format must be converted into dense numerical embeddings for a machine-learning classifier (e.g. identifying plant R proteins with LGBM), and pretrained deep representation learning models are available. Input is already a numerical feature table — this skill operates on raw FASTA sequences Sequences have not been redundancy-reduced; apply CD-HIT with a 30% identity cutoff first as in the source workflow Traditional hand-crafted features (e.g. k-spaced amino acid pairs as in prPred) are explicitly preferred or computational resources (GPU) are unavailable, since deep representation learning features require elevated computing resources http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 Encodes raw protein amino acid sequences into fixed-length numerical feature vectors using a pretrained BiLSTM deep representation learning embedding (3605D via eFeature), which in prPred-DRLF is fused with UniRep (1900D) embeddings to give a 5505-D input for plant R protein classification with an LGBM classifier. proteomics/v1 10.1002/pmic.202100161
skills.summary: Encodes raw protein amino acid sequences into fixed-length numerical feature vectors using a pretrained BiLSTM deep representation learning embedding (3605D via eFeature), which in prPred-DRLF is fused with UniRep (1900D) embeddings to give a 5505-D input for plant R protein classification with an LGBM classifier.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a numerical feature table — this skill operates on raw FASTA sequences Sequences have not been redundancy-reduced; apply CD-HIT with a 30% identity cutoff first as in the source workflow Traditional hand-crafted features (e.g. k-spaced amino acid pairs as in prPred) are explicitly preferred or computational resources (GPU) are unavailable, since deep representation learning features require elevated computing resources

Input is already a model comparison table or published metrics and the goal is to interpret, rather than re-run, the benchmark The task is multi-class classification rather than the binary positive/negative phosphosite prediction per residue model (ST, Y) No stratified train/validation/test split exists and cannot be constructed, since base-learner and ensemble metrics would not be comparable on the same held-out test set http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Benchmark binary classifiers on identical data splits by independently training each model variant outside the ensemble and comparing test-set metrics (AUPRC, AUROC, recall, F1). skills.description: Use when a muSignAl run yields many candidate biomarker signatures (e.g. 158 panels from Olink CVD-II in sign_cvd2.xlsx) and you must rank or threshold them by AUC to shortlist panels worth developing.

skills.search_text: biomarker-panel-prioritization Use when a muSignAl run yields many candidate biomarker signatures (e.g. 158 panels from Olink CVD-II in sign_cvd2.xlsx) and you must rank or threshold them by AUC to shortlist panels worth developing. The candidate signatures still need to be generated from the raw omics matrix — that is the upstream muSignAl run (test.R on the input .xlsx); this skill only prioritizes an existing final output like sign_cvd2.xlsx Only one candidate panel is under consideration — ranking by AUC adds no value without multiple alternative signatures The output has no per-signature performance metric (the AUC column computed with pROC is absent) — there is nothing to threshold or rank on http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Prioritizes candidate biomarker panels by ranking muSignAl-generated omic signatures on their predictive performance (AUC computed with pROC from glmnet-fitted models), e.g. isolating the 47 of 158 CVD-II proteomics signatures with AUC > 0.95. Because equally good multiple signatures let biomarker panel development cost be optimised, the ranked shortlist (Table 1, led by signature 150 at AUC 1.00) is the actionable artifact. proteomics/v1 10.1002/pmic.202200252
skills.summary: Prioritizes candidate biomarker panels by ranking muSignAl-generated omic signatures on their predictive performance (AUC computed with pROC from glmnet-fitted models), e.g. isolating the 47 of 158 CVD-II proteomics signatures with AUC > 0.95. Because equally good multiple signatures let biomarker panel development cost be optimised, the ranked shortlist (Table 1, led by signature 150 at AUC 1.00) is the actionable artifact.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The candidate signatures still need to be generated from the raw omics matrix — that is the upstream muSignAl run (test.R on the input .xlsx); this skill only prioritizes an existing final output like sign_cvd2.xlsx Only one candidate panel is under consideration — ranking by AUC adds no value without multiple alternative signatures The output has no per-signature performance metric (the AUC column computed with pROC is absent) — there is nothing to threshold or rank on

skills.description: Use when building an omic biomarker signature from a feature/sample matrix and you need a stability-based cutoff (feature frequency across resampled models) rather than a single-model coefficient ranking.
skills.name: biomarker-signature-thresholding
skills.search_text: biomarker-signature-thresholding Use when building an omic biomarker signature from a feature/sample matrix and you need a stability-based cutoff (feature frequency across resampled models) rather than a single-model coefficient ranking. The goal is to exhaustively explore all combinations of features — muSignAl is explicitly designed to bypass that requirement while finding multiple signatures with similar predictive performance The fitted subsample models do not exceed chance performance (AUC <= 0.5) — such models are discarded and provide no stable features to threshold A single deterministic model's coefficient ranking is sufficient, rather than resampling-based feature stability across 100 subsamples http://edamontology.org/topic_3577 Threshold-based biomarker feature selection as implemented in the muSignAl R package: feature importance (FI) is defined as the proportion of retained Elastic Net subsample models in which a feature appears, and features are kept when FI >= k (default 0.9) to form the first signature. proteomics/v1 10.1002/pmic.202200252
skills.summary: Threshold-based biomarker feature selection as implemented in the muSignAl R package: feature importance (FI) is defined as the proportion of retained Elastic Net subsample models in which a feature appears, and features are kept when FI >= k (default 0.9) to form the first signature.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is to exhaustively explore all combinations of features — muSignAl is explicitly designed to bypass that requirement while finding multiple signatures with similar predictive performance The fitted subsample models do not exceed chance performance (AUC <= 0.5) — such models are discarded and provide no stable features to threshold A single deterministic model's coefficient ranking is sufficient, rather than resampling-based feature stability across 100 subsamples

skills.description: Use when a CEST protocol is defined as a Pulseq .seq file and you need simulated Z-spectra to test or optimize the saturation preparation period in silico, or to validate simulations against measured Z-spectra.

skills.search_text: bloch-mcconnell-simulation Use when a CEST protocol is defined as a Pulseq .seq file and you need simulated Z-spectra to test or optimize the saturation preparation period in silico, or to validate simulations against measured Z-spectra. skills.summary: Run the pulseq-cest-sim open-source Bloch-McConnell simulation (C++ core exposed as a MATLAB mex-function or SWIG-wrapped Python package) on Pulseq .seq files to compute Z-spectra of CEST preparation periods in silico, so the same file played out on the scanner can be simulated and compared.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need an interpreter implementation for non-Siemens vendors — the Pulseq SBB is so far only available for Siemens scanners, though simulation itself remains vendor-independent You need quantitative in vivo Bloch-McConnell parameter maps — the article notes Bloch-McConnell based quantification is extremely challenging in vivo and its CEST-MRF is a work-in-progress method The saturation block is not defined in a Pulseq .seq file (e.g. proprietary vendor-specific sequence definitions)

skills.description: Use when training binary classifiers on datasets with strong positive/negative label imbalance (e.g., rare phosphorylation sites in plants) where recall on the minority class is the priority and standard training under-predicts positives.

skills.search_text: class-imbalance-weighted-training Use when training binary classifiers on datasets with strong positive/negative label imbalance (e.g., rare phosphorylation sites in plants) where recall on the minority class is the priority and standard training under-predicts positives. The dataset is already balanced or you are optimizing precision/AUPRC rather than recall — the article notes PhosBoost has a precision-recall tradeoff with increased predicted false positives compared to PhosphoLingo and DeepPhos. You only need a single learner and cannot afford per-classifier hyperparameter tuning — the balanced-weight base classifier alone scored lower AUPRC (.48) than the equal-weight one (.53) on the A. thaliana test set. The input is raw sequence without precomputed protein language model embeddings — this skill presupposes ProtT5 residue and protein-average embedding features. http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 http://edamontology.org/topic_3510 Train a balanced-weight classifier alongside an equal-weight classifier to handle severe class imbalance in phosphorylation prediction, then stack both with a logistic regression metaclassifier. PhosBoost uses this dual-CatBoost design because tyrosine phosphosites have far fewer positives than negatives, hurting recall. proteomics/v1 10.1002/pld3.554
skills.summary: Train a balanced-weight classifier alongside an equal-weight classifier to handle severe class imbalance in phosphorylation prediction, then stack both with a logistic regression metaclassifier. PhosBoost uses this dual-CatBoost design because tyrosine phosphosites have far fewer positives than negatives, hurting recall.

skills.description: Decision support for determining whether a numerical optimization routine (e.g., GrOpt ADMM gradient waveform design) is fast enough for on-the-fly use, and for quantifying how constraint sets change its asymptotic compute-time scaling with input size N.
skills.name: computational-complexity-scaling-analysis
skills.search_text: computational-complexity-scaling-analysis Decision support for determining whether a numerical optimization routine (e.g., GrOpt ADMM gradient waveform design) is fast enough for on-the-fly use, and for quantifying how constraint sets change its asymptotic compute-time scaling with input size N. The goal is validating whether a waveform is truly time-optimal — the article notes brute-force verification is computationally very expensive and out of scope here The optimizer output quality (e.g., residual gradient moments, intravoxel phase dispersion, ADC bias) is the target — that requires the numerical simulation workflow, not timing The routine's solution space convexity is the question — randomized-start tests are not a complete proof, so a scaling benchmark would not address it Empirically measures how an optimizer's compute time scales with problem size (waveform sample count N) by timing repeated optimization runs and fitting a power law t ~ N^alpha, and quantifies how adding constraints (e.g., a Schulte PNS constraint to GrOpt phase-contrast optimization) inflates the fitted exponent. proteomics/v1 10.1002/mrm.28384
skills.summary: Empirically measures how an optimizer's compute time scales with problem size (waveform sample count N) by timing repeated optimization runs and fitting a power law t ~ N^alpha, and quantifies how adding constraints (e.g., a Schulte PNS constraint to GrOpt phase-contrast optimization) inflates the fitted exponent.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is validating whether a waveform is truly time-optimal — the article notes brute-force verification is computationally very expensive and out of scope here The optimizer output quality (e.g., residual gradient moments, intravoxel phase dispersion, ADC bias) is the target — that requires the numerical simulation workflow, not timing The routine's solution space convexity is the question — randomized-start tests are not a complete proof, so a scaling benchmark would not address it

skills.description: Use when comparing drug sensitivity (AUC/IC50) between two cell-line subgroups defined by a discrete molecular alteration (e.g., mutated vs wild-type status of a user-defined gene) in GDSC, DepMap, or NCI60 pharmacogenomic data.
skills.name: discrete-omic-group-comparison-testing
skills.search_text: discrete-omic-group-comparison-testing Use when comparing drug sensitivity (AUC/IC50) between two cell-line subgroups defined by a discrete molecular alteration (e.g., mutated vs wild-type status of a user-defined gene) in GDSC, DepMap, or NCI60 pharmacogenomic data. The omics layer is continuous (mRNA, CNV, methylation, proteomics, metabolomics) — use Pearson or Spearman correlation with a coefficient threshold instead of a two-group test Drugs whose sensitivity values are 'NA' in greater than 15% of the cell lines have not yet been excluded — run that filter first or the group test will be underpowered/biased The goal is cis-/trans-regulation among omics levels or pathway activity correlation (GSVA-based), which are separate IMOPAC modules http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Group-comparison testing used within IMOPAC's drug–omics correlation analysis: for omics with discrete settings (e.g., somatic mutation status), cell lines are split into two subgroups by the mutation status of a user-defined gene and drug response (AUC/IC50) differences are tested with Wilcoxon's sign rank test or Student's t-test, with Benjamini–Hochberg correction across all tested gene–drug pairs. proteomics/v1 10.1016/j.csbj.2023.07.023
skills.summary: Group-comparison testing used within IMOPAC's drug–omics correlation analysis: for omics with discrete settings (e.g., somatic mutation status), cell lines are split into two subgroups by the mutation status of a user-defined gene and drug response (AUC/IC50) differences are tested with Wilcoxon's sign rank test or Student's t-test, with Benjamini–Hochberg correction across all tested gene–drug pairs.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The omics layer is continuous (mRNA, CNV, methylation, proteomics, metabolomics) — use Pearson or Spearman correlation with a coefficient threshold instead of a two-group test Drugs whose sensitivity values are 'NA' in greater than 15% of the cell lines have not yet been excluded — run that filter first or the group test will be underpowered/biased The goal is cis-/trans-regulation among omics levels or pathway activity correlation (GSVA-based), which are separate IMOPAC modules

skills.summary: Assigns FT-ICR MS-derived dissolved organic matter (DOM) molecular formulas to molecular classes (e.g., condensed aromatics, lignin) and labile/recalcitrant × active/inactive reactivity–activity fractions using the iDOM molGroup function, then aggregates relative abundance by class and fraction to identify dominant groups.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is raw mass spectra or peak lists without assigned molecular formulas — molGroup requires formula-level compositions to compute H/C and O/C traits The analysis goal is quantifying DOM assembly processes, dark matter effects, or DOM–microbe networks (use iDOM's commProc, iDME, or H2 functions instead) Assessing the compositional-level environmental (thermal) response of DOM, for which the iCER function is the intended tool

skills.description: Use when FT-ICR MS-derived DOM molecular formulae (with elemental compositions C, H, O, N, P, S) need per-molecule unsaturation descriptors — DBE, DBEO, DBEAI — as input to molecular-trait tables or chemical diversity analyses.
skills.name: double-bond-equivalent-estimation
skills.search_text: double-bond-equivalent-estimation Use when FT-ICR MS-derived DOM molecular formulae (with elemental compositions C, H, O, N, P, S) need per-molecule unsaturation descriptors — DBE, DBEO, DBEAI — as input to molecular-trait tables or chemical diversity analyses. Input is peak-level mass spectra (mzML or raw FT-ICR MS peaks) rather than already formula-assigned element composition data — molecular formula assignment must precede trait calculation Analysis target is DOM assembly processes, dark-matter effects, or DOM-microbe networks (iDOM's commProc, iDME, H2, iCER functions) rather than basic molecular trait calculation The dataset already contains computed DBE/unsaturation descriptors and only other traits are missing http://edamontology.org/topic_0153 http://edamontology.org/topic_3314 Calculates double bond equivalents (DBE) and its variants (DBEO, DBEAI) for dissolved organic matter (DOM) molecular formulas as part of the iDOM molTrait function, quantifying the degree of unsaturation of FT-ICR MS-assigned molecular formulae alongside related traits like the aromaticity index (AImod). proteomics/v1 10.1002/mlf2.70002
skills.summary: Calculates double bond equivalents (DBE) and its variants (DBEO, DBEAI) for dissolved organic matter (DOM) molecular formulas as part of the iDOM molTrait function, quantifying the degree of unsaturation of FT-ICR MS-assigned molecular formulae alongside related traits like the aromaticity index (AImod).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is peak-level mass spectra (mzML or raw FT-ICR MS peaks) rather than already formula-assigned element composition data — molecular formula assignment must precede trait calculation Analysis target is DOM assembly processes, dark-matter effects, or DOM-microbe networks (iDOM's commProc, iDME, H2, iCER functions) rather than basic molecular trait calculation The dataset already contains computed DBE/unsaturation descriptors and only other traits are missing

skills.description: Use when you want to identify gene–drug associations from multiomics and drug sensitivity matrices of GDSC, DepMap, or NCI60 cell lines in IMOPAC, for a user-defined gene of interest.
skills.name: drug-omics-correlation-analysis
skills.search_text: drug-omics-correlation-analysis Use when you want to identify gene–drug associations from multiomics and drug sensitivity matrices of GDSC, DepMap, or NCI60 cell lines in IMOPAC, for a user-defined gene of interest. The input omics is a fusion query, molecular classification, or pancancer expression analysis — IMOPAC has separate modules for those and this skill is not the right choice The user wants to correlate drug response with pathway activity computed by GSVA — the drug-pathway correlation analysis is a separate module The cell line set has fewer than ~85% drugs with sensitivity values, i.e. most drugs would be excluded by the 15% NA cutoff, leaving no usable associations http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3173 http://edamontology.org/topic_3517 Computes associations between the multiomics profile (e.g. mRNA, CNV, methylation, proteomics, metabolomics, somatic mutation) of a user-defined gene and drug sensitivity (AUC/IC50) across patient-derived cancer cell lines in IMOPAC, using Pearson/Spearman correlation for continuous omics and group tests for discrete omics. proteomics/v1 10.1016/j.csbj.2023.07.023
skills.summary: Computes associations between the multiomics profile (e.g. mRNA, CNV, methylation, proteomics, metabolomics, somatic mutation) of a user-defined gene and drug sensitivity (AUC/IC50) across patient-derived cancer cell lines in IMOPAC, using Pearson/Spearman correlation for continuous omics and group tests for discrete omics.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input omics is a fusion query, molecular classification, or pancancer expression analysis — IMOPAC has separate modules for those and this skill is not the right choice The user wants to correlate drug response with pathway activity computed by GSVA — the drug-pathway correlation analysis is a separate module The cell line set has fewer than ~85% drugs with sensitivity values, i.e. most drugs would be excluded by the 15% NA cutoff, leaving no usable associations

skills.search_text: dsf-data-analysis Use when analyzing DSF melting curves (e.g., from His-FGF10 thermal stability assays) to normalize, smooth, and extract Tm values from first derivative curves, including automated second-Tm recognition and unfolded/denatured classification. Data are raw DSF fluorescence traces not yet normalized or smoothed — run SimpleDSFviewer's normalization and smoothing steps first The goal is qualitative visual inspection only, without Tm extraction or automated peak-based screening http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Automated differential scanning fluorimetry (DSF) data analysis using SimpleDSFviewer, which integrates melting curve (MC) normalization, smoothing, and melting temperature (Tm) analysis with direct preview of analyzed results. skills.summary: Automated differential scanning fluorimetry (DSF) data analysis using SimpleDSFviewer, which integrates melting curve (MC) normalization, smoothing, and melting temperature (Tm) analysis with direct preview of analyzed results. Input is raw, unnormalized/unsmoothed DSF fluorescence — peak finding here expects FDCs already produced by SimpleDSFviewer's MC normalization and smoothing step Goal is manual or visual Tm estimation from a single known peak where second-Tm discrimination, no-Tm flagging, and unfolded-curve classification are not needed Data are not thermal melting curves from differential scanning fluorimetry (e.g. isothermal fluorescence or non-protein thermal stability assays) http://edamontology.org/topic_3361 Automated data-screening routine from SimpleDSFviewer that runs peak finding on normalized, smoothed first derivative curves (FDCs) from DSF melting curves to classify each curve as single-Tm, two-Tm, no-Tm (>=4 peaks), or unfolded/denatured (declining MC), reporting results to tm_screening_results.csv. proteomics/v1 10.1002/pro.3703
skills.summary: Automated data-screening routine from SimpleDSFviewer that runs peak finding on normalized, smoothed first derivative curves (FDCs) from DSF melting curves to classify each curve as single-Tm, two-Tm, no-Tm (>=4 peaks), or unfolded/denatured (declining MC), reporting results to tm_screening_results.csv.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw, unnormalized/unsmoothed DSF fluorescence — peak finding here expects FDCs already produced by SimpleDSFviewer's MC normalization and smoothing step Goal is manual or visual Tm estimation from a single known peak where second-Tm discrimination, no-Tm flagging, and unfolded-curve classification are not needed Data are not thermal melting curves from differential scanning fluorimetry (e.g. isothermal fluorescence or non-protein thermal stability assays)

The input traces are raw, un-normalized DSF fluorescence data that have not yet passed SimpleDSFviewer's melting curve (MC) normalization step The goal is melting temperature (Tm) estimation on already-smoothed curves, for which the Tm analysis module rather than the smoothing module is appropriate http://edamontology.org/topic_3292 Smoothing of normalized differential scanning fluorimetry (DSF) melting curves using SimpleDSFviewer's three-part module, which applies Matlab's smooth function segment-by-segment so the original curve shape is preserved for downstream Tm analysis. proteomics/v1 10.1002/pro.3703
skills.summary: Smoothing of normalized differential scanning fluorimetry (DSF) melting curves using SimpleDSFviewer's three-part module, which applies Matlab's smooth function segment-by-segment so the original curve shape is preserved for downstream Tm analysis.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input traces are raw, un-normalized DSF fluorescence data that have not yet passed SimpleDSFviewer's melting curve (MC) normalization step The goal is melting temperature (Tm) estimation on already-smoothed curves, for which the Tm analysis module rather than the smoothing module is appropriate

skills.description: Use when raw DSF fluorescence-versus-temperature melting curves (e.g. a 96-well plate) must be normalized, smoothed, and converted to per-well Tm values, or when checking whether smoothing perturbs FD-method Tm values.
skills.name: dsf-melting-curve-processing
skills.search_text: dsf-melting-curve-processing Use when raw DSF fluorescence-versus-temperature melting curves (e.g. a 96-well plate) must be normalized, smoothed, and converted to per-well Tm values, or when checking whether smoothing perturbs FD-method Tm values. Input fluorescence curves are already min-max normalized to the 0-1 range, so Equation 1 would be applied redundantly The analysis goal is not thermal stability (e.g. non-thermal interaction or kinetics modeling), which the MC normalization/smoothing/Tm pipeline is not designed for Implements the SimpleDSFviewer processing chain for differential scanning fluorimetry (DSF): per-well melting curve (MC) normalization (Equation 1), curve smoothing, and melting temperature (Tm) extraction via the first derivative curve (FDC). It turns raw fluorescence-versus-temperature plate data into normalized curves and per-well Tm tables. proteomics/v1 10.1002/pro.3703
skills.summary: Implements the SimpleDSFviewer processing chain for differential scanning fluorimetry (DSF): per-well melting curve (MC) normalization (Equation 1), curve smoothing, and melting temperature (Tm) extraction via the first derivative curve (FDC). It turns raw fluorescence-versus-temperature plate data into normalized curves and per-well Tm tables.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input fluorescence curves are already min-max normalized to the 0-1 range, so Equation 1 would be applied redundantly The analysis goal is not thermal stability (e.g. non-thermal interaction or kinetics modeling), which the MC normalization/smoothing/Tm pipeline is not designed for

skills.description: Use when you have raw DSF melting curves plus SimpleDSFviewer-smoothed counterparts (e.g. His-FGF7 + 50 µM heparin exemplar) and must verify smoothing preserves MC shape via per-point difference analysis.
skills.name: dsf-melting-curve-smoothing-comparison
skills.search_text: dsf-melting-curve-smoothing-comparison Use when you have raw DSF melting curves plus SimpleDSFviewer-smoothed counterparts (e.g. His-FGF7 + 50 µM heparin exemplar) and must verify smoothing preserves MC shape via per-point difference analysis. You only need melting temperature (Tm) values or MC normalization, not shape-preservation checks on smoothing — SimpleDSFviewer handles Tm analysis directly You lack both the raw and the smoothed MC versions of the same condition; difference analysis requires the paired curves on a shared temperature axis Input data come from a DSF analysis pipeline other than SimpleDSFviewer's built-in smoothing, so the reported 0.0392 / 2.517 benchmarks do not apply http://edamontology.org/topic_3334 http://edamontology.org/topic_3391 Quantifies point-wise differences between raw and smoothed differential scanning fluorimetry (DSF) melting curves to confirm that SimpleDSFviewer's MC smoothing preserves curve shape, benchmarking against reported extremes (0.0392 for folded protein flat areas; 2.517 for denatured-protein high peaks). proteomics/v1 10.1002/pro.3703
skills.summary: Quantifies point-wise differences between raw and smoothed differential scanning fluorimetry (DSF) melting curves to confirm that SimpleDSFviewer's MC smoothing preserves curve shape, benchmarking against reported extremes (0.0392 for folded protein flat areas; 2.517 for denatured-protein high peaks).
skills.when_to_use_negative: You only need melting temperature (Tm) values or MC normalization, not shape-preservation checks on smoothing — SimpleDSFviewer handles Tm analysis directly You lack both the raw and the smoothed MC versions of the same condition; difference analysis requires the paired curves on a shared temperature axis Input data come from a DSF analysis pipeline other than SimpleDSFviewer's built-in smoothing, so the reported 0.0392 / 2.517 benchmarks do not apply

skills.description: Use when the input is DSF fluorescence melting-curve data (e.g. a 96-well exemplar plate ramp) and the goal is to compute normalized FD curves, extract per-well Tm values, or compare Tm from smoothed vs unsmoothed MCs.
skills.name: dsf-thermal-stability-analysis
skills.search_text: dsf-thermal-stability-analysis Use when the input is DSF fluorescence melting-curve data (e.g. a 96-well exemplar plate ramp) and the goal is to compute normalized FD curves, extract per-well Tm values, or compare Tm from smoothed vs unsmoothed MCs. The input is not DSF melting-curve fluorescence data (e.g. it is a single-endpoint fluorescence readout with no temperature ramp, so no FDC or Tm can be defined). The temperature points of the ramp are non-uniform, so the central-difference formula FDC(n) = (MC(n+1) − MC(n−1)) / (2Δt) with a single Δt is invalid without per-pair spacing. The goal is protein–interaction quantification beyond thermal stability characterization, where this MC/FDC/Tm pipeline alone is not the analysis of record. Analyze differential scanning fluorimetry (DSF) melting curves with SimpleDSFviewer (a Matlab tool): normalize and smooth melting curves (MCs), compute first-derivative curves (FDCs) by central difference (Equation 2), and extract melting temperatures (Tm = temperature at max of FDC, Equation 3). proteomics/v1 10.1002/pro.3703
skills.summary: Analyze differential scanning fluorimetry (DSF) melting curves with SimpleDSFviewer (a Matlab tool): normalize and smooth melting curves (MCs), compute first-derivative curves (FDCs) by central difference (Equation 2), and extract melting temperatures (Tm = temperature at max of FDC, Equation 3).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is not DSF melting-curve fluorescence data (e.g. it is a single-endpoint fluorescence readout with no temperature ramp, so no FDC or Tm can be defined). The temperature points of the ramp are non-uniform, so the central-difference formula FDC(n) = (MC(n+1) − MC(n−1)) / (2Δt) with a single Δt is invalid without per-pair spacing. The goal is protein–interaction quantification beyond thermal stability characterization, where this MC/FDC/Tm pipeline alone is not the analysis of record.

skills.name: dssp-strip-table-generation
skills.search_text: dssp-strip-table-generation Use when you need per-residue standardized secondary-structure assignments (helices, ladders, sheets, turns, bends, chirality, exposure) computed from protein coordinate files and rendered as linear strip tables. DSSP does not predict secondary structure — do not use it for prediction from sequence; it requires 3D coordinate files with hydrogen-bond-capable geometry Input structures are not in mmCIF format and cannot be converted — the rewritten DSSP 4.6 offers full mmCIF support and writes annotated mmCIF output http://edamontology.org/topic_0736 http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 Generate DSSP strip tables — linear per-residue records of secondary structure, hydrogen-bonding, chirality, bend, and solvent exposure — for a set of globular proteins, reproducing the format of the Kabsch & Sander dictionary covering 62 proteins / 10,925 residues. proteomics/v1 10.1002/bip.360221211
skills.summary: Generate DSSP strip tables — linear per-residue records of secondary structure, hydrogen-bonding, chirality, bend, and solvent exposure — for a set of globular proteins, reproducing the format of the Kabsch & Sander dictionary covering 62 proteins / 10,925 residues.
skills.when_to_use_negative: DSSP does not predict secondary structure — do not use it for prediction from sequence; it requires 3D coordinate files with hydrogen-bond-capable geometry Input structures are not in mmCIF format and cannot be converted — the rewritten DSSP 4.6 offers full mmCIF support and writes annotated mmCIF output

skills.description: Use when quantitative DTI-derived targets (FA or MD maps) or input MR images are being prepared for training/testing the SC-GAN or baseline cGANs in the ADNI-3 FA/MD/PET synthesis tasks, where stable training requires intensities scaled between 0 and 1.
skills.name: dti-derived-quantitative-map-normalization
skills.search_text: dti-derived-quantitative-map-normalization Use when quantitative DTI-derived targets (FA or MD maps) or input MR images are being prepared for training/testing the SC-GAN or baseline cGANs in the ADNI-3 FA/MD/PET synthesis tasks, where stable training requires intensities scaled between 0 and 1. When absolute quantitative DTI metric values must be preserved (e.g., clinical MD/FA interpretation), since the authors note 'the normalization negatively affects the quantitative value of the metrics' and recommend avoiding it for quantitative modalities When the input is already intensity-normalized or the task targets non-quantitative structural images where rescaling provides no benefit When the claimed in-house result of no normalization dependency cannot be verified, since 'results are not presented' in the paper http://edamontology.org/topic_3444 http://edamontology.org/topic_3306 Applies Z-score normalization followed by min-max rescaling of voxel intensities to the 0-1 range for quantitative DTI-derived maps (fractional anisotropy, mean diffusivity) prior to GAN training in the SC-GAN multimodal synthesis workflow, so that target maps are in a stable range for network optimization. proteomics/v1 10.1002/mrm.28819
skills.summary: Applies Z-score normalization followed by min-max rescaling of voxel intensities to the 0-1 range for quantitative DTI-derived maps (fractional anisotropy, mean diffusivity) prior to GAN training in the SC-GAN multimodal synthesis workflow, so that target maps are in a stable range for network optimization.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When absolute quantitative DTI metric values must be preserved (e.g., clinical MD/FA interpretation), since the authors note 'the normalization negatively affects the quantitative value of the metrics' and recommend avoiding it for quantitative modalities When the input is already intensity-normalized or the task targets non-quantitative structural images where rescaling provides no benefit When the claimed in-house result of no normalization dependency cannot be verified, since 'results are not presented' in the paper

skills.description: Use when replicate concentration–response data from a targeted MS dilution series (e.g. SRM/MRM, PRM) must be reduced to a defensible linear range with LLOQ/ULOQ, instead of eyeballing response-factor plots.
skills.name: dynamic-linear-range-determination
skills.search_text: dynamic-linear-range-determination Use when replicate concentration–response data from a targeted MS dilution series (e.g. SRM/MRM, PRM) must be reduced to a defensible linear range with LLOQ/ULOQ, instead of eyeballing response-factor plots. Data are single-point or lack replicate measurements per concentration level, so MeasCV and PB_av/PB_cv cannot be computed The goal is inspection of raw chromatograms or transition intensities (e.g. Skyline) rather than calibration-curve statistics The concentration–response relationship is expected to be nonlinear over the full span and no linear sub-range is of interest http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Automated determination of the dynamic linear range (lower and upper limits of quantification) for targeted-MS calibration data using CalibraCurve, which assesses calibration accuracy via precision (PB_av, PB_cv, MeasCV) and trueness measures. proteomics/v1 10.1002/pmic.201900143
skills.summary: Automated determination of the dynamic linear range (lower and upper limits of quantification) for targeted-MS calibration data using CalibraCurve, which assesses calibration accuracy via precision (PB_av, PB_cv, MeasCV) and trueness measures.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Data are single-point or lack replicate measurements per concentration level, so MeasCV and PB_av/PB_cv cannot be computed The goal is inspection of raw chromatograms or transition intensities (e.g. Skyline) rather than calibration-curve statistics The concentration–response relationship is expected to be nonlinear over the full span and no linear sub-range is of interest

skills.description: Use when FT-ICR MS-derived DOM compositional data and molecular trait dendrograms (e.g. MCD, TD, TWCD) are available and the goal is to classify pairwise turnover into variable selection, homogeneous selection, or stochastic processes via betaNTI.
skills.name: ecological-null-model-interpretation
skills.search_text: ecological-null-model-interpretation Use when FT-ICR MS-derived DOM compositional data and molecular trait dendrograms (e.g. MCD, TD, TWCD) are available and the goal is to classify pairwise turnover into variable selection, homogeneous selection, or stochastic processes via betaNTI. Input lacks molecular trait information or a dendrogram relating DOM formulae, since betaNTI is dendrogram-based rather than phylogeny-based The goal is dark-matter effects on molecular interactions (use iDME) or DOM-microbe network specialization (use H2), not assembly-process quantification Only a single sample/community is available — betaNTI requires pairwise comparisons between assemblages http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Quantifies the relative influences of deterministic and stochastic processes in DOM assemblage assembly using dendrogram-based betaNTI null modeling implemented in the commProc function of the iDOM R package, applied to FT-ICR MS molecular data. proteomics/v1 10.1002/mlf2.70002
skills.summary: Quantifies the relative influences of deterministic and stochastic processes in DOM assemblage assembly using dendrogram-based betaNTI null modeling implemented in the commProc function of the iDOM R package, applied to FT-ICR MS molecular data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input lacks molecular trait information or a dendrogram relating DOM formulae, since betaNTI is dendrogram-based rather than phylogeny-based The goal is dark-matter effects on molecular interactions (use iDME) or DOM-microbe network specialization (use H2), not assembly-process quantification Only a single sample/community is available — betaNTI requires pairwise comparisons between assemblages

skills.search_text: elastic-net-feature-selection Use when a tabular omics matrix (e.g. Olink proteomics samples x features in .xlsx) must be reduced to predictive biomarker signatures via Elastic Net, with FI >= 0.9 cutoff and pROC AUC-based model filtering. When the goal is a single best-performing signature rather than multiple signatures with similar predictive performance When the input is not a samples x features omics matrix with a classifiable outcome (e.g. already-selected features or unstructured data) When exhaustive enumeration of all feature combinations is actually required rather than the FI-threshold shortcut http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Feature-importance-driven Elastic Net selection stage of the muSignAl algorithm: repeated glmnet model fitting (alpha = 0.9, 90% LASSO / 10% Ridge) over 100 random 80% subsamples defines feature importance (FI) as the proportion of retained models in which a feature appears, enabling enumeration of multiple omic signatures with similar predictive performance without exploring all feature combinations. proteomics/v1 10.1002/pmic.202200252
skills.summary: Feature-importance-driven Elastic Net selection stage of the muSignAl algorithm: repeated glmnet model fitting (alpha = 0.9, 90% LASSO / 10% Ridge) over 100 random 80% subsamples defines feature importance (FI) as the proportion of retained models in which a feature appears, enabling enumeration of multiple omic signatures with similar predictive performance without exploring all feature combinations.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is a single best-performing signature rather than multiple signatures with similar predictive performance When the input is not a samples x features omics matrix with a classifiable outcome (e.g. already-selected features or unstructured data) When exhaustive enumeration of all feature combinations is actually required rather than the FI-threshold shortcut

skills.search_text: f-beta-score-computation Use when comparing classifiers on imbalanced phosphosite predictions and you need to know which method wins when recall is prioritized over precision (beta > 1), not just at F1 or AUPRC. When the question is overall ranking by area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) rather than recall-prioritized performance — the article's AUPRC comparison (.54, .56, .42) is a different analysis When predictions are already hard labels and you need probability-threshold-free metrics like AUROC (all three S/T classifiers scored .88 AUROC, so AUROC cannot separate them here) http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Sweep the F-beta score over a grid of beta values (e.g. 0.25–3) using scikit-learn's fbeta_score to evaluate how phosphosite classifiers (PhosBoost, PhosphoLingo, DeepPhos) behave when recall is weighted more heavily than precision, reproducing the Figure 3d panel of the PhosBoost paper. proteomics/v1 10.1002/pld3.554

skills.when_to_use_negative: When the question is overall ranking by area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) rather than recall-prioritized performance — the article's AUPRC comparison (.54, .56, .42) is a different analysis When predictions are already hard labels and you need probability-threshold-free metrics like AUROC (all three S/T classifiers scored .88 AUROC, so AUROC cannot separate them here)

skills.description: Use when the goal is to predict DTI-derived FA volumes from structural multimodal MRI (T1w + FLAIR) with a 3D GAN, and when quantitative image-quality metrics (NRMSE, PSNR, SSIM) against ground-truth FA are the expected output.
skills.name: fa-map-synthesis-from-multimodal-mri
skills.search_text: fa-map-synthesis-from-multimodal-mri Use when the goal is to predict DTI-derived FA volumes from structural multimodal MRI (T1w + FLAIR) with a 3D GAN, and when quantitative image-quality metrics (NRMSE, PSNR, SSIM) against ground-truth FA are the expected output. When the target modality is a quantitative map whose absolute values matter (e.g., MD synthesis) and the 0–1 normalization step would distort the quantitative value of the metrics — the paper notes normalization 'negatively affects the quantitative value of the metrics' When no ground-truth FA maps or paired T1w/FLAIR data exist, since the conditional GAN requires paired multimodal input and target volumes for training and evaluation When GPU memory or training time is severely constrained — SC-GAN 'requires lengthy training and heavy computational resources, such as GPU memory' http://edamontology.org/topic_3444 http://edamontology.org/topic_3304 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Synthesize fractional anisotropy (FA) maps from co-registered T1w and FLAIR MRI using the 3D self-attention conditional GAN (SC-GAN) with spectral normalization, on ADNI-3 data (497 subjects: 398 training / 99 testing), achieving whole-brain NRMSE of 0.078/0.012 and 18% lower prediction error than a 2D conditional GAN. proteomics/v1 10.1002/mrm.28819
skills.summary: Synthesize fractional anisotropy (FA) maps from co-registered T1w and FLAIR MRI using the 3D self-attention conditional GAN (SC-GAN) with spectral normalization, on ADNI-3 data (497 subjects: 398 training / 99 testing), achieving whole-brain NRMSE of 0.078/0.012 and 18% lower prediction error than a 2D conditional GAN.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the target modality is a quantitative map whose absolute values matter (e.g., MD synthesis) and the 0–1 normalization step would distort the quantitative value of the metrics — the paper notes normalization 'negatively affects the quantitative value of the metrics' When no ground-truth FA maps or paired T1w/FLAIR data exist, since the conditional GAN requires paired multimodal input and target volumes for training and evaluation When GPU memory or training time is severely constrained — SC-GAN 'requires lengthy training and heavy computational resources, such as GPU memory'

skills.description: Use when a labeled protein dataset in FASTA format (e.g., plant R protein positives and negatives) must be deduplicated before feature extraction and classifier training.
skills.name: fasta-sequence-clustering
skills.search_text: fasta-sequence-clustering Use when a labeled protein dataset in FASTA format (e.g., plant R protein positives and negatives) must be deduplicated before feature extraction and classifier training. The input is already a feature table or embedding matrix (e.g., BiLSTM/UniRep vectors) rather than raw FASTA sequences — clustering is a sequence-level pre-step. The dataset is very small or sequences are already known to be non-redundant; aggressive 30% identity clustering could discard genuinely distinct homologs. The goal is family-level classification where sequence redundancy carries biological signal rather than being an artifact to remove. http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Removes redundant sequences from FASTA-format protein sets by clustering with CD-HIT at a low sequence-identity cutoff (30%) so that downstream machine-learning models are trained on non-redundant representatives. proteomics/v1 10.1002/pmic.202100161
skills.summary: Removes redundant sequences from FASTA-format protein sets by clustering with CD-HIT at a low sequence-identity cutoff (30%) so that downstream machine-learning models are trained on non-redundant representatives.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already a feature table or embedding matrix (e.g., BiLSTM/UniRep vectors) rather than raw FASTA sequences — clustering is a sequence-level pre-step. The dataset is very small or sequences are already known to be non-redundant; aggressive 30% identity clustering could discard genuinely distinct homologs. The goal is family-level classification where sequence redundancy carries biological signal rather than being an artifact to remove.

skills.description: Use when raw protein sequences downloaded from UniProt must be turned into a homology-reduced benchmark dataset in FASTA format before classifier training or cross-validation (e.g., sequences sharing >= 80% identity need to be collapsed).
skills.name: fasta-sequence-handling
skills.search_text: fasta-sequence-handling Use when raw protein sequences downloaded from UniProt must be turned into a homology-reduced benchmark dataset in FASTA format before classifier training or cross-validation (e.g., sequences sharing >= 80% identity need to be collapsed). The input FASTA has already been de-duplicated or homology-reduced at the required identity threshold (e.g., output of a prior CD-Hit run) The task is running the trained EMCBOW-GPCR predictor on a single FASTA file (use Predict.py instead of re-curation) The sequences are not protein sequences from the GPCR benchmark context and a different identity cutoff or clustering granularity is required http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 Curate a non-redundant FASTA protein dataset by downloading source sequences from UniProt and clustering them with CD-Hit at a 0.8 sequence identity threshold, keeping one representative per cluster. This reproduces the homology-reduced GPCR benchmark dataset used to evaluate EMCBOW-GPCR. proteomics/v1 10.1016/j.csbj.2021.08.044
skills.summary: Curate a non-redundant FASTA protein dataset by downloading source sequences from UniProt and clustering them with CD-Hit at a 0.8 sequence identity threshold, keeping one representative per cluster. This reproduces the homology-reduced GPCR benchmark dataset used to evaluate EMCBOW-GPCR.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input FASTA has already been de-duplicated or homology-reduced at the required identity threshold (e.g., output of a prior CD-Hit run) The task is running the trained EMCBOW-GPCR predictor on a single FASTA file (use Predict.py instead of re-curation) The sequences are not protein sequences from the GPCR benchmark context and a different identity cutoff or clustering granularity is required

skills.search_text: feature-ablation-sensitivity-analysis Use when a rescoring or classification pipeline adds engineered features and you must decide which features drive the performance gain, by retraining the model with subsets removed and comparing peptide counts at a fixed FDR. The goal is MHC-peptide binding affinity prediction rather than rescoring feature contribution (binding affinity used netMHCpan with percentile rank score <= 2% as binder definition) The aim is to compare search engines themselves rather than quantify feature contributions within a fixed rescoring framework No deep learning-derived features (RTdelta, SA) are available, so there is nothing to ablate against search-engine features http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Ablation analysis that quantifies how much each feature class (here, deep learning-derived delta RT and spectral angle) contributes to a rescoring model's peptide-identification gains, by retraining Percolator with feature subsets and comparing unique peptide counts at 1% FDR. proteomics/v1 10.1002/pmic.201900334
skills.summary: Ablation analysis that quantifies how much each feature class (here, deep learning-derived delta RT and spectral angle) contributes to a rescoring model's peptide-identification gains, by retraining Percolator with feature subsets and comparing unique peptide counts at 1% FDR.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is MHC-peptide binding affinity prediction rather than rescoring feature contribution (binding affinity used netMHCpan with percentile rank score <= 2% as binder definition) The aim is to compare search engines themselves rather than quantify feature contributions within a fixed rescoring framework No deep learning-derived features (RTdelta, SA) are available, so there is nothing to ablate against search-engine features

skills.description: Use when building omic feature-selection pipelines on high-dimensional datasets where stability of selected biomarkers across resampled models, not a single model's coefficients, should define feature importance.
skills.name: feature-importance-frequency-estimation
skills.search_text: feature-importance-frequency-estimation Use when building omic feature-selection pipelines on high-dimensional datasets where stability of selected biomarkers across resampled models, not a single model's coefficients, should define feature importance. The goal is a single best-performing signature rather than multiple signatures with similar predictive performance — muSignAl is designed to find several equally good signatures while bypassing exhaustive feature-combination search. Only a small number of resampled models is available, so the proportion-of-models FI estimate is unstable below the intended 100-subsample regime. The dataset is not suited to Elastic Net glmnet modeling (e.g. non-predictive labels), since models with AUC <= 0.5 are discarded and few models may survive. http://edamontology.org/topic_3577 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Estimates feature importance as the proportion of Elastic Net (glmnet, alpha=0.9) subsample models in which a feature appears, then selects features whose FI meets a threshold k=0.9, as used in the muSignAl signature-discovery workflow. proteomics/v1 10.1002/pmic.202200252
skills.summary: Estimates feature importance as the proportion of Elastic Net (glmnet, alpha=0.9) subsample models in which a feature appears, then selects features whose FI meets a threshold k=0.9, as used in the muSignAl signature-discovery workflow.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is a single best-performing signature rather than multiple signatures with similar predictive performance — muSignAl is designed to find several equally good signatures while bypassing exhaustive feature-combination search. Only a small number of resampled models is available, so the proportion-of-models FI estimate is unstable below the intended 100-subsample regime. The dataset is not suited to Elastic Net glmnet modeling (e.g. non-predictive labels), since models with AUC <= 0.5 are discarded and few models may survive.

skills.search_text: feature-importance-threshold-filtering Use when you need to enumerate multiple candidate biomarker signatures from a labeled omics dataset (e.g. proteomics matrix) without exploring all feature combinations, by ranking features with Elastic Net and applying an FI cutoff. When you need a single optimal signature and exhaustive combination search is computationally feasible When the input lacks a binary class label, since signatures are scored for predictive performance (AUC via pROC) http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 An approach from muSignAl that uses a feature-importance (FI) cutoff (e.g. k = 0.9) on glmnet-ranked features to enumerate multiple candidate omic signatures with similar predictive performance, instead of exhaustively testing all feature combinations. proteomics/v1 10.1002/pmic.202200252

skills.description: Use when training a conditional GAN (e.g., SC-GAN for MRI/PET/DTI synthesis) and the generator loss must include a feature matching term alongside the cGAN adversarial loss, L1 loss, and brain-area RMSE loss to stabilize training.
skills.name: feature-matching-loss-implementation
skills.search_text: feature-matching-loss-implementation Use when training a conditional GAN (e.g., SC-GAN for MRI/PET/DTI synthesis) and the generator loss must include a feature matching term alongside the cGAN adversarial loss, L1 loss, and brain-area RMSE loss to stabilize training. Input is plain image-to-image regression where adversarial training is not desired — the 3D Unet-style supervised path suffices without the discriminator feature space The task already ships a verified reference loss module from github.com/Haoyulance/SC-GAN; reuse it rather than reimplementing Training is memory- or time-constrained: SC-GAN requires lengthy training and heavy GPU memory, so a lighter loss configuration may be preferable http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Implements the feature matching loss term of the SC-GAN generator objective for 3D multimodal neuroimaging synthesis, where the discriminator's intermediate feature activations anchor the generator's adversarial training. Together with spectral normalization, feature matching is what stabilizes SC-GAN training and ensures optimization convergence. proteomics/v1 10.1002/mrm.28819

Together with spectral normalization, feature matching is what stabilizes SC-GAN training and ensures optimization convergence.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is plain image-to-image regression where adversarial training is not desired — the 3D Unet-style supervised path suffices without the discriminator feature space The task already ships a verified reference loss module from github.com/Haoyulance/SC-GAN; reuse it rather than reimplementing Training is memory- or time-constrained: SC-GAN requires lengthy training and heavy GPU memory, so a lighter loss configuration may be preferable

skills.search_text: feature-vector-concatenation-fusion Use when multiple per-sequence embedding vectors (e.g. BiLSTM 3605D and UniRep 1900D from eFeature) must be merged into one fixed-width feature matrix before classifier training, with exact dimensionality checks. Input is already a single fixed-width feature table — no additional embeddings to fuse exist Only one embedding model was run (e.g. TAPE-BERT 768D alone) and there is no second vector to concatenate Feature matrices have different sequence rows/IDs that cannot be aligned — concatenation would mislabel proteins http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Per-sequence fusion of deep representation learning protein embeddings by column-wise concatenation: in prPred-DRLF, a 3605D BiLSTM embedding and a 1900D UniRep embedding are merged into a single 5505D feature vector per protein for plant R protein identification. proteomics/v1 10.1002/pmic.202100161

skills.description: Use when you have smoothed, normalized DSF melting curves (MCs) sampled at a uniform temperature increment and need the first-derivative curve (FDC) whose peak marks each well's melting temperature.
skills.name: fluorescence-curve-normalization
skills.search_text: fluorescence-curve-normalization Use when you have smoothed, normalized DSF melting curves (MCs) sampled at a uniform temperature increment and need the first-derivative curve (FDC) whose peak marks each well's melting temperature. The melting curves are still raw fluorescence and have not passed SimpleDSFviewer's normalization and smoothing steps — the FD formula assumes normalized, smoothed MC input The assay does not provide a uniform temperature increment (dt) between neighboring measurement points, so the central-difference denominator 2*dt is undefined You only need Tm peak calling from an already-computed FDC and do not need to reconstruct the derivative curve itself Computes the first-derivative curve (FDC) from normalized, smoothed differential scanning fluorimetry (DSF) melting curves using SimpleDSFviewer's central-difference Equation (2), then normalizes the FDC with the same procedure as the MCs so derivative amplitudes are comparable across wells for melting-temperature (Tm) analysis. proteomics/v1 10.1002/pro.3703
skills.summary: Computes the first-derivative curve (FDC) from normalized, smoothed differential scanning fluorimetry (DSF) melting curves using SimpleDSFviewer's central-difference Equation (2), then normalizes the FDC with the same procedure as the MCs so derivative amplitudes are comparable across wells for melting-temperature (Tm) analysis.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The melting curves are still raw fluorescence and have not passed SimpleDSFviewer's normalization and smoothing steps — the FD formula assumes normalized, smoothed MC input The assay does not provide a uniform temperature increment (dt) between neighboring measurement points, so the central-difference denominator 2*dt is undefined You only need Tm peak calling from an already-computed FDC and do not need to reconstruct the derivative curve itself
