skills.name: fluorescence-melting-curve-quality-interpretation
skills.search_text: fluorescence-melting-curve-quality-interpretation Decision support for validating DSF melting-temperature calls across a multi-well plate: when per-well HMD and FD Tm values must be joined and discrepancy classes (averaged two-species Tm, not-calculable Tm) flagged before reporting results. Melting curves containing only a single protein species with low initial fluorescence — HMD and FD will agree and no discrepancy analysis is needed Analysis goals that need only normalized or smoothed curves (SimpleDSFviewer's MC normalization/smoothing) rather than Tm-method cross-validation Datasets from instruments/file formats other than the DSF fluorescence melting curves supported by SimpleDSFviewer/Matlab Interprets differential scanning fluorimetry (DSF) melting curves by comparing half-maximal-derivative (HMD) Tm values against first-derivative (FD) Tm values to flag curves the HMD method handles incorrectly, e.g. two-species curves that yield a single averaged Tm or high-initial-fluorescence curves where Tm is not calculable. proteomics/v1 10.1002/pro.3703
skills.summary: Interprets differential scanning fluorimetry (DSF) melting curves by comparing half-maximal-derivative (HMD) Tm values against first-derivative (FD) Tm values to flag curves the HMD method handles incorrectly, e.g. two-species curves that yield a single averaged Tm or high-initial-fluorescence curves where Tm is not calculable.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Melting curves containing only a single protein species with low initial fluorescence — HMD and FD will agree and no discrepancy analysis is needed Analysis goals that need only normalized or smoothed curves (SimpleDSFviewer's MC normalization/smoothing) rather than Tm-method cross-validation Datasets from instruments/file formats other than the DSF fluorescence melting curves supported by SimpleDSFviewer/Matlab

skills.name: focal-loss-binary-classification-training
skills.search_text: focal-loss-binary-classification-training Use when a high-dimensional concatenated feature vector (e.g., 1011-D word-embedding + bag-of-words GPCR features) must be reduced via a trained DL module whose Layer-1 output is the final representation. Input is already a reduced 505-D feature table produced by Layer-1 interception — feed it directly to XGBoost instead The task is multi-class GPCR family prediction rather than the binary GPCR identification setup with focal loss / binary cross-entropy CBOW models have not been trained and raw sequences must first be converted to word-embedding and BOW features http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Train a small deep-learning network (three fully connected layers, two Batch Normalization layers, Leaky ReLU activations) on concatenated GPCR feature vectors (1011-D) using focal loss / binary cross-entropy with the Adam optimizer (learning rate 0.01), and intercept the 505-D Layer-1 output as dimension-reduced features for downstream XGBoost. proteomics/v1 10.1016/j.csbj.2021.08.044
skills.summary: Train a small deep-learning network (three fully connected layers, two Batch Normalization layers, Leaky ReLU activations) on concatenated GPCR feature vectors (1011-D) using focal loss / binary cross-entropy with the Adam optimizer (learning rate 0.01), and intercept the 505-D Layer-1 output as dimension-reduced features for downstream XGBoost.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a reduced 505-D feature table produced by Layer-1 interception — feed it directly to XGBoost instead The task is multi-class GPCR family prediction rather than the binary GPCR identification setup with focal loss / binary cross-entropy CBOW models have not been trained and raw sequences must first be converted to word-embedding and BOW features

skills.description: Use when iTRAQ/TMT/TMTpro-labeled PSMs need interference QC scores computed per scan from b/y fragment ion intensity fractions in mzML data, to filter compressed reporter ion quantifications.
skills.name: fragment-ion-intensity-scoring
skills.search_text: fragment-ion-intensity-scoring Use when iTRAQ/TMT/TMTpro-labeled PSMs need interference QC scores computed per scan from b/y fragment ion intensity fractions in mzML data, to filter compressed reporter ion quantifications. Input is a protein-level feature table or already-filtered quantification matrix — the scores must be computed per scan prior to protein-level quantification. Data are label-free or use non-isobaric labeling (the score calculations revolve around iTRAQ/TMT/TMTpro reporter and complementary ion series). Only MS1 precursor purity assessment is needed — ms1PrecSignal is a limited predictor of reporter ion interference (a majority of scans show 100% even when accuracy is reduced), so fragment-ion scores would be the correct choice, but the reverse (using ms1PrecSignal alone) is the mistake. http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Compute IsobaricQuant fragment-ion-based QC scores (peptideIntensityScore and peptideTopXIntensityFromTotalScore) by matching b/y fragment ions, including neutral losses 63.98, 18.01 and 17.03, against MS2/MS3 scan peaks to quantify the fraction of scan intensity explained by the target peptide, enabling filtering of scans with co-isolation (ratio compression). proteomics/v1 10.1002/pmic.202100253
skills.summary: Compute IsobaricQuant fragment-ion-based QC scores (peptideIntensityScore and peptideTopXIntensityFromTotalScore) by matching b/y fragment ions, including neutral losses 63.98, 18.01 and 17.03, against MS2/MS3 scan peaks to quantify the fraction of scan intensity explained by the target peptide, enabling filtering of scans with co-isolation (ratio compression).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is a protein-level feature table or already-filtered quantification matrix — the scores must be computed per scan prior to protein-level quantification. Data are label-free or use non-isobaric labeling (the score calculations revolve around iTRAQ/TMT/TMTpro reporter and complementary ion series). Only MS1 precursor purity assessment is needed — ms1PrecSignal is a limited predictor of reporter ion interference (a majority of scans show 100% even when accuracy is reduced), so fragment-ion scores would be the correct choice, but the reverse (using ms1PrecSignal alone) is the mistake.

skills.summary: Extract per-spectrum fragment-ion m/z and intensity values from the SupportData instances exposed by the XTandem Parser Java object model after parsing an X!Tandem XML result file.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is not X!Tandem XML output (e.g. MASCOT .dat or OMSSA result files) — those have their own parsers (Mascot-Dat File, OMSSA Parser) The goal is cross-search-engine visualization/analysis of results — use PeptideShaker, the search-engine-independent platform the authors recommend Only search input parameters or modification settings are needed without ion-level data — the InputParams and ModificationMap objects suffice without touching SupportData

skills.description: Use when you have X!Tandem XML result files and need to export detailed per-spectrum identification fields (peptide, E-value, hyperscore, protein accession, spectrum details) into a spreadsheet-openable format.
skills.name: fragment-spectrum-metadata-extraction
skills.search_text: fragment-spectrum-metadata-extraction Use when you have X!Tandem XML result files and need to export detailed per-spectrum identification fields (peptide, E-value, hyperscore, protein accession, spectrum details) into a spreadsheet-openable format. Input files are MASCOT or OMSSA result files — use Mascot-Dat File or OMSSA Parser instead, since XTandem Parser is specific to X!Tandem XML output. You need interactive GUI-based visualization/analysis of X!Tandem results rather than scripted bulk export — the authors recommend PeptideShaker as a search-engine independent platform for visualization and analysis. You only need to view a single spectrum interactively — the bundled XTandem Viewer GUI (built on SwingX, JGoodies, and compomics-utilities) is designed for that rather than writing a parser script. http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Extracts detailed per-spectrum identification metadata (peptide sequence, E-value, hyperscore, protein accession, charge, precursor m/z, fragment ion m/z/intensity) from X!Tandem XML output files into a tab-delimited table using the XTandem Parser Java library. proteomics/v1 10.1002/pmic.200900759
skills.summary: Extracts detailed per-spectrum identification metadata (peptide sequence, E-value, hyperscore, protein accession, charge, precursor m/z, fragment ion m/z/intensity) from X!Tandem XML output files into a tab-delimited table using the XTandem Parser Java library.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input files are MASCOT or OMSSA result files — use Mascot-Dat File or OMSSA Parser instead, since XTandem Parser is specific to X!Tandem XML output. You need interactive GUI-based visualization/analysis of X!Tandem results rather than scripted bulk export — the authors recommend PeptideShaker as a search-engine independent platform for visualization and analysis. You only need to view a single spectrum interactively — the bundled XTandem Viewer GUI (built on SwingX, JGoodies, and compomics-utilities) is designed for that rather than writing a parser script.

skills.description: Use when an FT-ICR MS molecule-by-sample compositional matrix contains low-prevalence molecules and downstream statistics (e.g., Spearman MER vs. temperature, iCER thermal response) require a prevalence-filtered abundance table.
skills.name: fticr-ms-compositional-data-filtering
skills.search_text: fticr-ms-compositional-data-filtering Use when an FT-ICR MS molecule-by-sample compositional matrix contains low-prevalence molecules and downstream statistics (e.g., Spearman MER vs. temperature, iCER thermal response) require a prevalence-filtered abundance table. The analysis goal is DOM assembly processes, dark matter effects, or DOM-microbe networks (use iDOM's commProc, iDME, or H2 functions instead of iCER-based filtering) The input is already a matrix of molecular traits, molecular classes, or dark matter rather than a raw molecule-by-sample compositional matrix The dataset lacks an environmental gradient (e.g., temperature) to correlate molecular relative abundances against, so MER computation is undefined Prevalence-based filtering of FT-ICR MS molecular compositional matrices (retaining molecules detected in >=30% of samples) prior to computing molecule-level environmental responses (MER) and the sample-level iCER indicator with the iDOM R package. proteomics/v1 10.1002/mlf2.70002
skills.summary: Prevalence-based filtering of FT-ICR MS molecular compositional matrices (retaining molecules detected in >=30% of samples) prior to computing molecule-level environmental responses (MER) and the sample-level iCER indicator with the iDOM R package.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The analysis goal is DOM assembly processes, dark matter effects, or DOM-microbe networks (use iDOM's commProc, iDME, or H2 functions instead of iCER-based filtering) The input is already a matrix of molecular traits, molecular classes, or dark matter rather than a raw molecule-by-sample compositional matrix The dataset lacks an environmental gradient (e.g., temperature) to correlate molecular relative abundances against, so MER computation is undefined

skills.search_text: fticr-ms-elemental-ratio-categorization Use when an FT-ICR MS DOM peak/formula table (e.g., molecular formulae with elemental composition) needs categorical molecular class and reactivity–activity fraction assignment for compositional summarization. The data are raw FT-ICR MS spectra or unassigned peaks without molecular formulae — formula assignment must precede class categorization The goal is quantifying DOM assembly processes, dark-matter effects, or DOM–microbe networks — iDOM's commProc, iDME, or H2 functions, not molGroup, are the appropriate entry points The input is already a categorized class/fraction table; recomputation would not add information http://edamontology.org/topic_2258 http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Assigns FT-ICR MS-derived molecular formulae to DOM molecular classes (e.g., condensed aromatics/ConHC, lignin, CHO/CHON formula groups) and labile/recalcitrant × active/inactive reactivity–activity fractions using iDOM's molGroup function in R, based on molecular traits such as H/C and O/C ratios. proteomics/v1 10.1002/mlf2.70002
skills.summary: Assigns FT-ICR MS-derived molecular formulae to DOM molecular classes (e.g., condensed aromatics/ConHC, lignin, CHO/CHON formula groups) and labile/recalcitrant × active/inactive reactivity–activity fractions using iDOM's molGroup function in R, based on molecular traits such as H/C and O/C ratios.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The data are raw FT-ICR MS spectra or unassigned peaks without molecular formulae — formula assignment must precede class categorization The goal is quantifying DOM assembly processes, dark-matter effects, or DOM–microbe networks — iDOM's commProc, iDME, or H2 functions, not molGroup, are the appropriate entry points The input is already a categorized class/fraction table; recomputation would not add information

skills.description: Use when FT-ICR MS yields a samples-by-molecular-formula compositional table (presence/absence plus relative abundance) and the goal is molecular traits, class assignment, diversity indices, dissimilarity matrices, or region/temperature comparisons of DOM composition.
skills.name: fticr-ms-molecular-composition-analysis
skills.search_text: fticr-ms-molecular-composition-analysis Use when FT-ICR MS yields a samples-by-molecular-formula compositional table (presence/absence plus relative abundance) and the goal is molecular traits, class assignment, diversity indices, dissimilarity matrices, or region/temperature comparisons of DOM composition. Input is raw FT-ICR MS peak/feature output that has not yet been converted to a samples-by-formula compositional table — molecular traits and class assignment in iDOM operate on compositional data, not spectra The goal is quantifying DOM assembly processes (commProc), dark-matter co-occurrence effects (iDME), or DOM-microbe bipartite network specialization (H2) — these are separate advanced iDOM functions outside this composition/diversity skill Data are taxonomic (ASV/OTU) rather than molecular formula composition; iDOM's chemical diversity and dissimilarity functions target FT-ICR MS DOM data Analyzes dissolved organic matter (DOM) molecular composition from FT-ICR MS using the iDOM R package: computing molecular traits, assigning molecular classes, and quantifying chemical diversity (richness, Shannon, evenness, RaoQ, MNTD) and sample-by-sample dissimilarity (Jaccard, Bray-Curtis, UniFrac) for downstream ordination and PERMANOVA testing. proteomics/v1 10.1002/mlf2.70002
skills.summary: Analyzes dissolved organic matter (DOM) molecular composition from FT-ICR MS using the iDOM R package: computing molecular traits, assigning molecular classes, and quantifying chemical diversity (richness, Shannon, evenness, RaoQ, MNTD) and sample-by-sample dissimilarity (Jaccard, Bray-Curtis, UniFrac) for downstream ordination and PERMANOVA testing.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw FT-ICR MS peak/feature output that has not yet been converted to a samples-by-formula compositional table — molecular traits and class assignment in iDOM operate on compositional data, not spectra The goal is quantifying DOM assembly processes (commProc), dark-matter co-occurrence effects (iDME), or DOM-microbe bipartite network specialization (H2) — these are separate advanced iDOM functions outside this composition/diversity skill Data are taxonomic (ASV/OTU) rather than molecular formula composition; iDOM's chemical diversity and dissimilarity functions target FT-ICR MS DOM data

skills.description: Use when you have an FT-ICR MS molecular compositional table (molecules x samples with relative abundances) plus assigned molecular traits, and need a functional diversity index per sample to test trait-based responses (e.g., to warming).
skills.name: functional-diversity-raoq-cwm-estimation
skills.search_text: functional-diversity-raoq-cwm-estimation Use when you have an FT-ICR MS molecular compositional table (molecules x samples with relative abundances) plus assigned molecular traits, and need a functional diversity index per sample to test trait-based responses (e.g., to warming). Input is only a peak list without relative abundances — CWM weighting of traits by abundance cannot be computed Molecules have no assigned molecular traits or classes, so no trait space exists for RaoQ/MNTD computation The goal is purely compositional (taxonomic-equivalent) richness/Shannon/evenness rather than trait-weighted functional diversity — use iDOM's basic diversity functions instead http://edamontology.org/topic_0157 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Estimate the functional diversity of dissolved organic matter (DOM) assemblages by computing Rao's quadratic entropy (RaoQ) through community-weighted means (CWM), weighting molecular traits (e.g., H/C, O/C-derived trait values) by the relative abundances of assigned FT-ICR MS molecules. proteomics/v1 10.1002/mlf2.70002
skills.summary: Estimate the functional diversity of dissolved organic matter (DOM) assemblages by computing Rao's quadratic entropy (RaoQ) through community-weighted means (CWM), weighting molecular traits (e.g., H/C, O/C-derived trait values) by the relative abundances of assigned FT-ICR MS molecules.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is only a peak list without relative abundances — CWM weighting of traits by abundance cannot be computed Molecules have no assigned molecular traits or classes, so no trait space exists for RaoQ/MNTD computation The goal is purely compositional (taxonomic-equivalent) richness/Shannon/evenness rather than trait-weighted functional diversity — use iDOM's basic diversity functions instead

skills.description: Use when a task requires reconstructing or coding a 3D conditional GAN (generator, discriminator, self-attention blocks, spectral normalization) and its composite loss from an architecture description, e.g., MRI/PET synthesis.
skills.name: gan-architecture-implementation
skills.search_text: gan-architecture-implementation Use when a task requires reconstructing or coding a 3D conditional GAN (generator, discriminator, self-attention blocks, spectral normalization) and its composite loss from an architecture description, e.g., MRI/PET synthesis. The task is 2D slice-wise synthesis — the article shows 2D conditional GAN has 18–29% higher prediction error than SC-GAN on 3D volumes, but if only 2D data exist this 3D architecture is unnecessary. A pretrained or off-the-shelf model suffices and no architectural reconstruction or modification is required. The target task is conventional regression (e.g., 3D U-ET-style segmentation/synthesis) where GAN training instability cannot be tolerated — SC-GAN requires heavy GPU memory and lengthy training. http://edamontology.org/topic_3444 http://edamontology.org/topic_3384 Implements the SC-GAN architecture: a 3D conditional GAN generator and discriminator, each with a 3D self-attention module and spectral normalization, plus the composite loss (adversarial cGAN, L1 μ=200, feature matching λ, brain-area RMSE γ=200, and L2 regularization νG=νD=0.001) for multimodal neuroimaging synthesis. proteomics/v1 10.1002/mrm.28819
skills.summary: Implements the SC-GAN architecture: a 3D conditional GAN generator and discriminator, each with a 3D self-attention module and spectral normalization, plus the composite loss (adversarial cGAN, L1 μ=200, feature matching λ, brain-area RMSE γ=200, and L2 regularization νG=νD=0.001) for multimodal neuroimaging synthesis.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The task is 2D slice-wise synthesis — the article shows 2D conditional GAN has 18–29% higher prediction error than SC-GAN on 3D volumes, but if only 2D data exist this 3D architecture is unnecessary. A pretrained or off-the-shelf model suffices and no architectural reconstruction or modification is required. The target task is conventional regression (e.g., 3D U-ET-style segmentation/synthesis) where GAN training instability cannot be tolerated — SC-GAN requires heavy GPU memory and lengthy training.

skills.when_to_use_negative: Synthesizing quantitative modalities (e.g., DTI metrics) when preserving absolute quantitative values matters — the 0–1 min-max rescaling of target images negatively affects quantitative DTI metric values When training time or GPU memory is severely constrained — computational cost (lengthy training, heavy GPU memory) is the main limitation of SC-GAN Tasks requiring 2D slice-wise synthesis where 3D consistency is not needed — 2D conditional GAN is a lighter alternative (SC-GAN prediction error was 18–29% lower, but at higher compute cost)

The goal is benchmarking SC-GAN against other architectures (2D conditional GAN, 3D conditional GAN, 3D U-Net) rather than decomposing SC-GAN's own components — use the comparative-evaluation workflow instead Only a single trained model and limited compute are available — the paper notes computational cost (lengthy training, heavy GPU memory) is SC-GAN's main limitation, making five retraining runs infeasible The synthesis task involves quantitative modalities where 0–1 normalization distorts metric values and training stability differs from the PET/DTI tasks studied http://edamontology.org/topic_3444 http://edamontology.org/topic_3384 A method for quantifying which components of a GAN (e.g., SC-GAN's self-attention, adversarial loss, B-rmse, spectral normalization, feature matching) drive synthesis performance by training one variant per removed component and ranking metric degradation on a held-out test set. proteomics/v1 10.1002/mrm.28819

skills.search_text: gan-hyperparameter-tuning-cross-validation Use when training conditional GANs (SC-GAN, 2D/3D cGAN, Att cGAN) on 256x256x256 medical images and you need to select hyperparameters (mu, lambda, lr, batch size) fairly via cross-validation before benchmarking. skills.summary: Tunes and compares GAN architectures for 3D neuroimaging synthesis by sweeping regularization weights, learning rates and batch sizes under 5-fold cross-validation, then benchmarking on held-out subjects with NRMSE, peak SNR and SSIM. Grounded in the SC-GAN study on ADNI-3 PET/FA/MD synthesis from T1w and FLAIR MRI.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The task is not image-to-image synthesis from MRI but classification/regression or data already reduced to feature tables — the tuning targets voxel-level GAN training. skills.description: Decision support for choosing between HMD and FD Tm determination when analyzing 96-well DSF melting curves — especially heparin-binding thermal shift data where curves may contain two protein species of different Tm values or high initial fluorescence.
skills.name: heparin-protein-thermal-shift-interpretation
skills.search_text: heparin-protein-thermal-shift-interpretation Decision support for choosing between HMD and FD Tm determination when analyzing 96-well DSF melting curves — especially heparin-binding thermal shift data where curves may contain two protein species of different Tm values or high initial fluorescence. The melting curve is a simple single-species transition — HMD and FD will agree and the comparison adds no information. The goal is routine normalization/smoothing/previewing of melting curves rather than HMD-vs-FD Tm discrepancy assessment (SimpleDSFviewer's core MC normalization, smoothing, and Tm-analysis functions suffice). Input data are not DSF fluorescence-versus-temperature melting curves (e.g. already-summarized Tm tables with no raw curves). Interprets 96-well differential scanning fluorimetry (DSF) melting curves of heparin–protein interactions by comparing HMD (half-maximal denaturation) Tm values against FD (first derivative) Tm values, flagging the two known HMD failure modes: curves containing two protein species with different Tm values (where HMD yields a single averaged Tm) and high-initial-fluorescence curves where HMD cannot calculate a Tm at all. proteomics/v1 10.1002/pro.3703
skills.summary: Interprets 96-well differential scanning fluorimetry (DSF) melting curves of heparin–protein interactions by comparing HMD (half-maximal denaturation) Tm values against FD (first derivative) Tm values, flagging the two known HMD failure modes: curves containing two protein species with different Tm values (where HMD yields a single averaged Tm) and high-initial-fluorescence curves where HMD cannot calculate a Tm at all.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The melting curve is a simple single-species transition — HMD and FD will agree and the comparison adds no information. The goal is routine normalization/smoothing/previewing of melting curves rather than HMD-vs-FD Tm discrepancy assessment (SimpleDSFviewer's core MC normalization, smoothing, and Tm-analysis functions suffice). Input data are not DSF fluorescence-versus-temperature melting curves (e.g. already-summarized Tm tables with no raw curves).

Bottom-up digested peptides where sequence-level distinction (not PTM positional isomers) is the goal; the README recommends the software for middle-down or top-down analyses with scrambled combinatorial PTMs Input is raw Mascot .xml output that has not been validated and nomenclature-converted by Histone Coder — isoScale requires the Histone Coder result file as input http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Quantify histone peptides and resolve co-fragmenting isobaric species by computing the fragment ion relative ratio (FIRR) from total MS/MS ion intensity, using isoScale on Mascot/Histone Coder output from middle-down ETD data. proteomics/v1 10.1002/pmic.201400084
skills.summary: Quantify histone peptides and resolve co-fragmenting isobaric species by computing the fragment ion relative ratio (FIRR) from total MS/MS ion intensity, using isoScale on Mascot/Histone Coder output from middle-down ETD data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Bottom-up digested peptides where sequence-level distinction (not PTM positional isomers) is the goal; the README recommends the software for middle-down or top-down analyses with scrambled combinatorial PTMs Input is raw Mascot .xml output that has not been validated and nomenclature-converted by Histone Coder — isoScale requires the Histone Coder result file as input

skills.description: Use when TMT/iTRAQ PSM quantification tables are impaired by precursor co-isolation (ratio compression) and you need to remove inaccurate peptide quantifications at MS2 or MS3 level before protein-level aggregation.
skills.name: isobaric-peptide-qc-score-filtering
skills.search_text: isobaric-peptide-qc-score-filtering Use when TMT/iTRAQ PSM quantification tables are impaired by precursor co-isolation (ratio compression) and you need to remove inaccurate peptide quantifications at MS2 or MS3 level before protein-level aggregation. When the RTS-MS3 acquisition method was set to a maximum of 2 PSMs per protein, since this significantly limits the possibility of filtering peptides When filtering would be applied after protein-level quantification — the article states filtering must occur directly prior to protein-level quantification so protein inference is not impacted When ms1PrecSignal is the only available QC score, since a majority of scans show 100% even when quantitative accuracy is reduced http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Filter isobarically-labeled (TMT/iTRAQ/TMTpro) peptide quantifications suffering from co-isolation interference using IsobaricQuant QC scores (e.g., peptideTopXIntensityFromTotalScore with cutoff 0.15 at MS3 level), while applying a two-peptide minimum protection rule so protein-level CVs decrease without depleting protein observations. proteomics/v1 10.1002/pmic.202100253
skills.summary: Filter isobarically-labeled (TMT/iTRAQ/TMTpro) peptide quantifications suffering from co-isolation interference using IsobaricQuant QC scores (e.g., peptideTopXIntensityFromTotalScore with cutoff 0.15 at MS3 level), while applying a two-peptide minimum protection rule so protein-level CVs decrease without depleting protein observations.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the RTS-MS3 acquisition method was set to a maximum of 2 PSMs per protein, since this significantly limits the possibility of filtering peptides When filtering would be applied after protein-level quantification — the article states filtering must occur directly prior to protein-level quantification so protein inference is not impacted When ms1PrecSignal is the only available QC score, since a majority of scans show 100% even when quantitative accuracy is reduced

skills.description: Use when validating that a new or custom reporter-ion quantification tool produces intensities consistent with established software (FragPipe, MaxQuant) on isobarically-labeled TMT/TMTpro data acquired at MS2 or MS3 level.
skills.name: isobaric-quantification-cross-tool-benchmarking
skills.search_text: isobaric-quantification-cross-tool-benchmarking Use when validating that a new or custom reporter-ion quantification tool produces intensities consistent with established software (FragPipe, MaxQuant) on isobarically-labeled TMT/TMTpro data acquired at MS2 or MS3 level. The goal is filtering inaccurate quantifications rather than benchmarking tool agreement — use IsobaricQuant QC scores (msnTotalSignal cutoff 1e6 for MS2; peptideIntensityScore 0.25 or peptideTopXIntensityFromTotalScore 0.15 for MS3) instead The data are label-free or use labels other than iTRAQ (up to 8-plex), TMT (up to 11-plex), or TMTpro (up to 16-plex), which IsobaricQuant does not support Only one quantification tool is available, so no cross-tool correlation benchmark is possible http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Benchmark IsobaricQuant reporter-ion quantification against FragPipe and MaxQuant on the HYpro16 TMTpro 16-plex dataset (PXD020815) across MS2, SPS-MS3, and RTS-MS3 acquisition methods, verifying agreement via Pearson correlations of log10 reporter intensities on shared scan groups. proteomics/v1 10.1002/pmic.202100253
skills.summary: Benchmark IsobaricQuant reporter-ion quantification against FragPipe and MaxQuant on the HYpro16 TMTpro 16-plex dataset (PXD020815) across MS2, SPS-MS3, and RTS-MS3 acquisition methods, verifying agreement via Pearson correlations of log10 reporter intensities on shared scan groups.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is filtering inaccurate quantifications rather than benchmarking tool agreement — use IsobaricQuant QC scores (msnTotalSignal cutoff 1e6 for MS2; peptideIntensityScore 0.25 or peptideTopXIntensityFromTotalScore 0.15 for MS3) instead The data are label-free or use labels other than iTRAQ (up to 8-plex), TMT (up to 11-plex), or TMTpro (up to 16-plex), which IsobaricQuant does not support Only one quantification tool is available, so no cross-tool correlation benchmark is possible

skills.description: Use when quantifying TMT/TMTpro/iTRAQ reporter ions from mzML spectra plus PSM hits, or when filtering isobarically-labeled scans suffering precursor interference/compression prior to protein-level quantification.
skills.name: isobaric-reporter-ion-quantification
skills.search_text: isobaric-reporter-ion-quantification Use when quantifying TMT/TMTpro/iTRAQ reporter ions from mzML spectra plus PSM hits, or when filtering isobarically-labeled scans suffering precursor interference/compression prior to protein-level quantification. The data are label-free or not labeled with iTRAQ/TMT/TMTpro isobaric tags, or the plex exceeds supported limits (iTRAQ 8-plex, TMT 11-plex, TMTpro 16-plex). You need to identify the co-isolated peptides and their reporter ion release efficiency to perform ratio decompression — IsobaricQuant cannot resolve these, it only scores interference. Input is already a protein-level feature table; filtering must be applied at the scan/peptide level directly prior to protein-level quantification. http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 IsobaricQuant is a Java-based, cross-platform tool that quantifies iTRAQ (up to 8-plex), TMT (up to 11-plex), and TMTpro (up to 16-plex) reporter ion intensities from mzML files and computes QC scores (ms1PrecSignal, msnTotalSignal, peptideIntensityScore, peptideTopXIntensityFromTotalScore) to filter scans with compression from co-isolated precursors. proteomics/v1 10.1002/pmic.202100253
skills.summary: IsobaricQuant is a Java-based, cross-platform tool that quantifies iTRAQ (up to 8-plex), TMT (up to 11-plex), and TMTpro (up to 16-plex) reporter ion intensities from mzML files and computes QC scores (ms1PrecSignal, msnTotalSignal, peptideIntensityScore, peptideTopXIntensityFromTotalScore) to filter scans with compression from co-isolated precursors.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The data are label-free or not labeled with iTRAQ/TMT/TMTpro isobaric tags, or the plex exceeds supported limits (iTRAQ 8-plex, TMT 11-plex, TMTpro 16-plex). You need to identify the co-isolated peptides and their reporter ion release efficiency to perform ratio decompression — IsobaricQuant cannot resolve these, it only scores interference. Input is already a protein-level feature table; filtering must be applied at the scan/peptide level directly prior to protein-level quantification.

skills.description: Use when quantifying TMT, TMTpro, or iTRAQ reporter ions from mzML files with a search-engine PSM table, especially when co-isolation interference may distort ratios and scan-level filtering is desired.
skills.name: isobaric-tmt-peptide-quantification
skills.search_text: isobaric-tmt-peptide-quantification Use when quantifying TMT, TMTpro, or iTRAQ reporter ions from mzML files with a search-engine PSM table, especially when co-isolation interference may distort ratios and scan-level filtering is desired. skills.summary: Quantify, visualize, and filter isobarically-labeled (iTRAQ/TMT/TMTpro) peptides with IsobaricQuant, a Java 17 standalone tool that computes per-scan QC scores to remove reporter-ion interference at MS2 and MS3 levels prior to protein-level aggregation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The data are not isobarically labeled (e.g. label-free or SILAC quantification) or labels are outside iTRAQ 8-plex / TMT 11-plex / TMTpro 16-plex Only a protein-level feature table exists and scan-level reporter-ion quantification cannot be re-run from mzML and PSM hits RTS-MS3 acquisition collected very few PSMs per protein (e.g. max 2), leaving too little redundancy for filtering to help

skills.description: Use when peptide-spectrum matches from Morpheus contain peptides shared across multiple proteins, and abundance estimates are needed for protein families or isoforms/proteoforms rather than only individually resolved proteins.
skills.name: isoform-proteoform-abundance-estimation
skills.search_text: isoform-proteoform-abundance-estimation Use when peptide-spectrum matches from Morpheus contain peptides shared across multiple proteins, and abundance estimates are needed for protein families or isoforms/proteoforms rather than only individually resolved proteins. The data were not searched with the Morpheus Mass Spectrometry Search Engine — MSpC requires Morpheus output and cannot parse other engines' results The analysis targets individually resolved proteins only and shared-peptide ambiguity is irrelevant, in which case a single plain NSAF computation suffices Quantification requires MS1 peak-based (feature-intensity) methods rather than spectral counting http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Estimates label-free protein abundance for protein families and isoforms/proteoforms by computing distributed NSAF (spectral counts of shared peptides divided among family members) and unique NSAF (counts from family-member-exclusive peptides) directly from Morpheus search-engine output using MSpC. proteomics/v1 10.1002/pmic.201500420
skills.summary: Estimates label-free protein abundance for protein families and isoforms/proteoforms by computing distributed NSAF (spectral counts of shared peptides divided among family members) and unique NSAF (counts from family-member-exclusive peptides) directly from Morpheus search-engine output using MSpC.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The data were not searched with the Morpheus Mass Spectrometry Search Engine — MSpC requires Morpheus output and cannot parse other engines' results The analysis targets individually resolved proteins only and shared-peptide ambiguity is irrelevant, in which case a single plain NSAF computation suffices Quantification requires MS1 peak-based (feature-intensity) methods rather than spectral counting

skills.summary: Renders raw MS visualizations of an LC-MS/MS run — a retention-time vs m/z ion-intensity heat map, 3D m/z × retention-time × intensity maps of MS1 survey and MS2 fragmentation scans, and a zoomed view of a peptide's isotopic envelope — directly from on-disk raw data using mzR, reproducing Figure 3 of Gatto et al. 2015.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already processed, e.g. identification results in mzid files or a feature/quantitation table — use Pbase/MSnSet-level visualization instead of raw scan rendering The goal is protein/peptide-level exploration of sequences and mapped peptide ranges, which is Pbase's Proteins-object workflow rather than raw-run visualization No R/Bioconductor environment is available and the data must be explored interactively in vendor raw-file software

skills.search_text: itraq-4plex-ms2-spectrum-overlay-visualization Use when raw MS2 spectra of one identified peptide exist at multiple precursor charge states (e.g. iTRAQ 4-plex) and the goal is an overlaid, fragment-annotated comparison plot in R. Input is already a processed/quantitative matrix (e.g. an MSnSet feature table) rather than raw MS2 spectra — the skill operates on the MSnExp raw-data abstraction Only one charge state of the peptide is available, so the charge-2 vs charge-3 overlay comparison is impossible The goal is protein/peptide mapping against FASTA sequences (the Pbase Proteins object workflow with HUMAN_2015_02_selected.fasta and Thermo_Hela_PRTC_selected.mzid) rather than raw spectrum visualization http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Uses R/Bioconductor (Pbase/MSnbase data abstraction plus protViz-style annotation) to overlay two MS2 spectra of the same peptide — IMIDLDGTENK from an iTRAQ 4-plex experiment — at precursor charge states 2 and 3, reproducing the central panel of Figure 4 of Gatto et al. 2015. proteomics/v1 10.1002/pmic.201400392
skills.summary: Uses R/Bioconductor (Pbase/MSnbase data abstraction plus protViz-style annotation) to overlay two MS2 spectra of the same peptide — IMIDLDGTENK from an iTRAQ 4-plex experiment — at precursor charge states 2 and 3, reproducing the central panel of Figure 4 of Gatto et al. 2015.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a processed/quantitative matrix (e.g. an MSnSet feature table) rather than raw MS2 spectra — the skill operates on the MSnExp raw-data abstraction Only one charge state of the peptide is available, so the charge-2 vs charge-3 overlay comparison is impossible The goal is protein/peptide mapping against FASTA sequences (the Pbase Proteins object workflow with HUMAN_2015_02_selected.fasta and Thermo_Hela_PRTC_selected.mzid) rather than raw spectrum visualization

skills.search_text: java-interface-implementation Use when building Java software that must read several MS peak list formats (e.g. for mzIdentML consumers) and you want one parser interface (lookup by index, ID, scan number) instead of per-format code paths. The input is a single fixed file format only — using the abstraction layer adds indirection without benefit. The client must access format-specific metadata not exposed by the common interface (e.g. raw mzData binary block internals). Working outside the JVM — the jmzReader parsers are Java APIs and cannot be used directly from other runtimes. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Implement a single common Java interface (as in jmzReader) behind which multiple format-specific parsers expose identical operations, so client code supports one API instead of many file formats. In jmzReader, all peak list parsers (DTA, MS2, MGF, PKL, mzXML, mzData, mzML) share one interface that supports mzIdentML's external spectra referencing methods. proteomics/v1 10.1002/pmic.201100578
skills.summary: Implement a single common Java interface (as in jmzReader) behind which multiple format-specific parsers expose identical operations, so client code supports one API instead of many file formats. In jmzReader, all peak list parsers (DTA, MS2, MGF, PKL, mzXML, mzData, mzML) share one interface that supports mzIdentML's external spectra referencing methods.

skills.search_text: java-library-benchmarking Use when you must measure how fast and how memory-light a Java parser runs on XML result files of increasing size — e.g. X!Tandem output files with 3225, 60902, or 233327 quality spectra — against a published reference. The goal is visualizing or biologically analyzing the X!Tandem identifications rather than benchmarking the parser (PeptideShaker is recommended for that). The input is not X!Tandem XML output — Mascot DAT files and OMSSA result files are handled by other parsers (Mascot-Dat File, OMSSA Parser). You need the X!Tandem search itself performed, not its output parsed; use the X!Tandem search engine (e.g. via SearchGUI) for searching. http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Benchmark the wall-clock parsing time and peak memory of a Java library on files of graded sizes, as done for XTandem Parser on X!Tandem XML result files containing 3225, 60902 and 233327 quality spectra. Rationale: performance claims for bioinformatics parsers should be reproducible against published reference tables. proteomics/v1 10.1002/pmic.200900759
skills.summary: Benchmark the wall-clock parsing time and peak memory of a Java library on files of graded sizes, as done for XTandem Parser on X!Tandem XML result files containing 3225, 60902 and 233327 quality spectra. Rationale: performance claims for bioinformatics parsers should be reproducible against published reference tables.

skills.search_text: lc-msms-biomarker-list-filtering Use when MALDI imaging proteolytic peaks (m/z [M+H]+ list) need to be annotated against LC-MS/MS proteomic discovery data, and a gene-name cluster list must first be used to restrict candidate biomarkers before correlation matching. skills.summary: Restricts LC-MS/MS-based proteomic biomarker discovery data to a gene-name list of interest (e.g., the HSIL(+) cluster) so that MALDI imaging [M+H]+ peaks can be matched only against candidate biomarkers, using the MALDImID R package/Shiny app for more specific peak identification.

Input is MALDI imaging peak data rather than the LC-MS/MS peptide mass reference table — that data follows a different path (peak picking and proton-mass conversion) in the MALDImID workflow A matched_masses.csv output table already exists and only validation of ±0.2 Da mass differences is required http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Loads and parses the LC-MS/MS-derived peptide mass table (peptides.txt) so that MALDI imaging m/z peaks can be matched against experimentally identified peptide masses within the MALDImID workflow. This parsing step supplies the reference mass list that the MALDImID R package and Shiny app exploit for more specific identification of MALDI imaging proteolytic peaks. proteomics/v1 10.1002/pmic.202300005
skills.summary: Loads and parses the LC-MS/MS-derived peptide mass table (peptides.txt) so that MALDI imaging m/z peaks can be matched against experimentally identified peptide masses within the MALDImID workflow. skills.description: Use when you have a high-dimensional fused protein embedding (e.g., 5505D BiLSTM+UniRep vectors from FASTA sequences) and need feature selection plus a strong classifier for binary protein-family prediction with accuracy/F1/AUC evaluation.

skills.search_text: lgbm-feature-selection-and-classification Use when you have a high-dimensional fused protein embedding (e.g., 5505D BiLSTM+UniRep vectors from FASTA sequences) and need feature selection plus a strong classifier for binary protein-family prediction with accuracy/F1/AUC evaluation. Input is already a compact, curated feature table — LGBM importance ranking over a 5505D fused embedding is unnecessary and may discard informative dimensions Sequences are highly redundant — apply CD-HIT with a 30% identity cutoff first or metrics will be inflated by near-duplicate sequences HMMER-style profile/domain annotation is the goal; note the article's caveat that HMMER evaluation was restricted to the positive training set because most negative-set sequences were incompletely annotated http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 Applies a Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LGBM) both as a feature-importance ranker to extract an optimal subset from high-dimensional fused protein embeddings and as the final classifier for plant R protein (R vs non-R) prediction, as in prPred-DRLF. proteomics/v1 10.1002/pmic.202100161

skills.search_text: local-window-deviation-calculation Use when you have an X-ray protein structure in PDB format and need to detect residues whose mobility (Cα B-factor) deviates from their local sequence neighborhood, e.g. for protein-ligand interaction analysis. skills.description: Use when validating that a new reporter-ion quantification tool produces intensities consistent with tools, by reprocessing the same mzML files with multiple tools and correlating their log10 reporter intensities on shared scan groups.
skills.name: log10-reporter-intensity-correlation-analysis
skills.search_text: log10-reporter-intensity-correlation-analysis Use when validating that a new reporter-ion quantification tool produces intensities consistent with tools, by reprocessing the same mzML files with multiple tools and correlating their log10 reporter intensities on shared scan groups. The input data are not isobarically labeled (iTRAQ/TMT/TMTpro) — reporter-ion quantification tools are not applicable to label-free data. The goal is to assess quantitative accuracy of individual scans (ratio compression) rather than cross-tool intensity agreement; use IsobaricQuant QC-score filtering instead. Plex sizes exceed tool support (IsobaricQuant supports up to iTRAQ 8-plex, TMT 11-plex, TMTpro 16-plex). http://edamontology.org/topic_0082 http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Benchmark a novel isobaric quantification tool against established software (FragPipe, MaxQuant) by joining reporter ion intensities on shared scan groups and computing pairwise Pearson correlations of log10-transformed reporter intensities. Applied here to validate IsobaricQuant on the HYpro16 TMTpro 16-plex dataset across MS2, SPS-MS3, and RTS-MS3 acquisition methods. proteomics/v1 10.1002/pmic.202100253
skills.summary: Benchmark a novel isobaric quantification tool against established software (FragPipe, MaxQuant) by joining reporter ion intensities on shared scan groups and computing pairwise Pearson correlations of log10-transformed reporter intensities. Applied here to validate IsobaricQuant on the HYpro16 TMTpro 16-plex dataset across MS2, SPS-MS3, and RTS-MS3 acquisition methods.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input data are not isobarically labeled (iTRAQ/TMT/TMTpro) — reporter-ion quantification tools are not applicable to label-free data. The goal is to assess quantitative accuracy of individual scans (ratio compression) rather than cross-tool intensity agreement; use IsobaricQuant QC-score filtering instead. Plex sizes exceed tool support (IsobaricQuant supports up to iTRAQ 8-plex, TMT 11-plex, TMTpro 16-plex).

skills.description: Use when search-engine PSMs need a retention-time-based rescoring feature: Prosit iRT predictions for confident target PSMs must be mapped through a LOWESS fit to observed RT so ΔRT deviations can separate correct from incorrect PSMs.
skills.name: lowess-curve-fitting
skills.search_text: lowess-curve-fitting Use when search-engine PSMs need a retention-time-based rescoring feature: Prosit iRT predictions for confident target PSMs must be mapped through a LOWESS fit to observed RT so ΔRT deviations can separate correct from incorrect PSMs. Do not assume LOWESS is active by default: the Oktoberfest regressionMethod config default is "spline", so a practitioner wanting LOWESS must explicitly set it; conversely, if the spline or logistic regression fit is desired, this skill's specific LOWESS path is not the right configuration. If the goal is spectral library generation or collision energy calibration (the other Oktoberfest job types) rather than ΔRT feature computation for rescoring, this skill does not apply. If no experimentally observed retention times are available (e.g. peptides without search-engine PSM hits), there is nothing to align against and ΔRT cannot be computed. http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Fits a locally weighted scatterplot smoothing (LOWESS) curve to align Prosit-predicted iRT values with experimentally observed retention times from search engine results, then computes per-PSM ΔRT (predicted minus observed RT) as a feature for data-driven PSM rescoring in the Oktoberfest pipeline. proteomics/v1 10.1002/pmic.202300112
skills.summary: Fits a locally weighted scatterplot smoothing (LOWESS) curve to align Prosit-predicted iRT values with experimentally observed retention times from search engine results, then computes per-PSM ΔRT (predicted minus observed RT) as a feature for data-driven PSM rescoring in the Oktoberfest pipeline.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Do not assume LOWESS is active by default: the Oktoberfest regressionMethod config default is "spline", so a practitioner wanting LOWESS must explicitly set it; conversely, if the spline or logistic regression fit is desired, this skill's specific LOWESS path is not the right configuration. If the goal is spectral library generation or collision energy calibration (the other Oktoberfest job types) rather than ΔRT feature computation for rescoring, this skill does not apply. If no experimentally observed retention times are available (e.g. peptides without search-engine PSM hits), there is nothing to align against and ΔRT cannot be computed.

skills.description: Use when the goal is to visualize log2 reporter-intensity ratios between two TMT channels (e.g. TMT129 or TMT131 vs TMT127) as MA scatter plots, especially to contrast R's base, lattice and ggplot2 plotting systems on the same data.
skills.name: ma-plot-construction
skills.search_text: ma-plot-construction Use when the goal is to visualize log2 reporter-intensity ratios between two TMT channels (e.g. TMT129 or TMT131 vs TMT127) as MA scatter plots, especially to contrast R's base, lattice and ggplot2 plotting systems on the same data. Input is already a summary figure or feature table without per-feature reporter-ion intensities, so per-feature log2 ratios M and averages A cannot be computed The task requires a single quantitative-accuracy criterion against the published figure — the source only defines a qualitative visual check Channels other than the TMT129/TMT131 vs TMT127 comparisons of PXD000001 are needed without recomputing M and A from the relevant reporter-ion columns http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Reproduces the MA plots of Figure 1 from Gatto et al. (PROTEOMICS, 2015), where the PXD000001 TMT 6-plex reporter-ion data (HeLa/PRTC run on a Thermo Orbitrap Q Exactive) is plotted as M (log2 fold change) versus A (average log2 intensity) three times — once with each of R's three plotting systems (traditional/base, lattice, ggplot2) — to compare their syntax and output on identical proteomics data. proteomics/v1 10.1002/pmic.201400392
skills.summary: Reproduces the MA plots of Figure 1 from Gatto et al. skills.search_text: magnetic-resonance-fingerprinting-dictionary-matching Use when quantitative CEST parameter maps (fMT, kMT, fAmide, kAmide) must be derived from spin-lock-based CEST-MRF acquisitions, especially for cross-site or multi-scanner reproducibility studies. When the goal is only qualitative APT-weighted imaging or Z-spectrum comparison without quantitative exchange-parameter estimation When the scanner vendor does not support the Pulseq sequence building block (SBB so far only available for Siemens scanners; interpreter software for Philips, United or Canon is needed) When in vivo Bloch-McConnell-based absolute quantification is required with strict accuracy claims — the article notes such quantification is extremely challenging in vivo http://edamontology.org/topic_3418 Generates Bloch-McConnell signal dictionaries from spin-lock-based CEST-MRF pulseq sequences (amide-weighted and semi-solid MTC schedules) and matches measured voxel-wise Z-spectra against them to compute quantitative exchange parameter maps (fMT, kMT, fAmide, kAmide) across multiple MR sites. proteomics/v1 10.1002/mrm.28825

skills.description: Use when the goal is to simulate, compare, or optimize CEST pre-saturation protocols defined as Pulseq .seq-files — e.g., predicting the Z-spectrum of an APTw preparation block before scanner time, or checking that a shared protocol behaves as expected.
skills.name: magnetization-transfer-pool-modeling
skills.search_text: magnetization-transfer-pool-modeling Use when the goal is to simulate, compare, or optimize CEST pre-saturation protocols defined as Pulseq .seq-files — e.g., predicting the Z-spectrum of an APTw preparation block before scanner time, or checking that a shared protocol behaves as expected. The input is raw scanner k-space or image data rather than a Pulseq .seq-file — this skill simulates the preparation block only, not image reconstruction or post-processing. You need in vivo Bloch-McConnell-based quantification — the article notes this is 'extremely challenging in vivo'; the simulation is for protocol testing/optimization, not quantitative pool-size fitting of patient data. The sequence of interest cannot be expressed as a Pulseq saturation block (e.g., vendor-native sequences without a Pulseq interpreter). http://edamontology.org/topic_3384 Configure and run a Bloch-McConnell magnetization-exchange simulation of CEST saturation blocks defined in Pulseq .seq-files, modeling one or more CEST pools plus a semi-solid MTC pool to produce a Z-spectrum in silico. This enables testing and optimization of CEST preparation periods using the exact same .seq file that is played out on the scanner. proteomics/v1 10.1002/mrm.28825
skills.summary: Configure and run a Bloch-McConnell magnetization-exchange simulation of CEST saturation blocks defined in Pulseq .seq-files, modeling one or more CEST pools plus a semi-solid MTC pool to produce a Z-spectrum in silico. This enables testing and optimization of CEST preparation periods using the exact same .seq file that is played out on the scanner.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is raw scanner k-space or image data rather than a Pulseq .seq-file — this skill simulates the preparation block only, not image reconstruction or post-processing. You need in vivo Bloch-McConnell-based quantification — the article notes this is 'extremely challenging in vivo'; the simulation is for protocol testing/optimization, not quantitative pool-size fitting of patient data. The sequence of interest cannot be expressed as a Pulseq saturation block (e.g., vendor-native sequences without a Pulseq interpreter).

skills.summary: Parsing Mascot (Matrix Science) database-search outputs into the formats consumed by the middle-down proteomics tools: Mascot .xml feeds Histone Coder for PTM-localization validation, and a Histone Coder result file plus Mascot .csv data file feed isoScale for MS/MS total-ion-intensity quantification of combinatorially modified histone peptides.

The goal is bottom-up peptide quantification from MS1 precursor intensities or spectral counting alone — isoScale is explicitly recommended for middle-down or top-down analyses of single sequences with scrambled combinatorial PTMs. PTMs outside the Histone Coder scope (e.g. ubiquitination, glycation on residues other than the supported S/T/Y, K, R methylation states) are present and cannot be handled by the built-in modification list.

skills.search_text: metaproteomics-search-space-comparison Use when a MaxQuant (or similar) search over large or growing FASTA search spaces (e.g. metaproteomics against Swiss-Prot plus IGC) yields collapsing PSM counts, and you want to quantify how deep-learning-based rescoring restores identifications. Input is DIA data or a spectral-library-generation/collision-energy-calibration job, not a MaxQuant search-results rescoring task Search results come from a search engine other than MaxQuant without an Oktoberfest conversion path, or spectra are not RAW/mzML for the FTMS profile assumed by the 20 ppm fragment tolerance No Koina server access is available for Prosit predictions, since feature generation depends on predicted fragment intensities http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Reproduces the Oktoberfest-based data-driven rescoring analysis on the metaproteomics dataset PXD010871 searched against increasingly large search spaces (Swiss-Prot Human, +Bacteria, +IGC), showing that Prosit/mokapot rescoring with Koina-predicted fragment intensities largely rescues the PSM loss that MaxQuant suffers as the search space grows. proteomics/v1 10.1002/pmic.202300112
skills.summary: Reproduces the Oktoberfest-based data-driven rescoring analysis on the metaproteomics dataset PXD010871 searched against increasingly large search spaces (Swiss-Prot Human, +Bacteria, +IGC), showing that Prosit/mokapot rescoring with Koina-predicted fragment intensities largely rescues the PSM loss that MaxQuant suffers as the search space grows.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is DIA data or a spectral-library-generation/collision-energy-calibration job, not a MaxQuant search-results rescoring task Search results come from a search engine other than MaxQuant without an Oktoberfest conversion path, or spectra are not RAW/mzML for the FTMS profile assumed by the 20 ppm fragment tolerance No Koina server access is available for Prosit predictions, since feature generation depends on predicted fragment intensities

skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already normalized melting-curve output (values within [0, 1] per curve) from a prior SimpleDSFviewer run The goal is Tm extraction on raw unnormalized curves rather than producing the 0–1 scaled MC used downstream The data are not DSF fluorescence-versus-temperature melting curves (e.g. isothermal fluorescence reads or spectra), where per-curve min-max scaling has no melting-curve interpretation

skills.search_text: multiple-sequence-alignment-residue-tallying Use when a multiple sequence alignment (e.g. a MUSCLE-aligned FASTA of protein variants) must be converted into per-position amino acid occurrence counts and percentages to build a consensus or conservation report. The input is a DNA/SNP-variant analysis scenario: scop3D then produces a matrix annotating the protein sequence with SNP frequency, variants and variant type instead of amino acid occurrence matrices Only a single unaligned sequence is available and no multiple sequence alignment has been produced with MUSCLE yet The goal is structural annotation (PDB B-value replacement with percent conservation or entropy) rather than per-position amino acid composition reporting http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Reconstructs scop3D's per-position amino acid occurrence computation: after aligning protein sequence variants with MUSCLE, tally absolute and relative abundances of every amino acid at each alignment position and write them as two separate text matrices. skills.summary: Reconstructs scop3D's per-position amino acid occurrence computation: after aligning protein sequence variants with MUSCLE, tally absolute and relative abundances of every amino acid at each alignment position and write them as two separate text matrices. This underpins consensus-sequence construction and downstream 3D conservation mapping.

skills.description: Use when benchmarking Oktoberfest rescoring runtime across raw-file combinations of varying PSM counts, or when deciding whether enabling multiprocessing for prediction/rescoring is worth it.
skills.name: multiprocessing-parallel-configuration
skills.search_text: multiprocessing-parallel-configuration Use when benchmarking Oktoberfest rescoring runtime across raw-file combinations of varying PSM counts, or when deciding whether enabling multiprocessing for prediction/rescoring is worth it. The goal is identification sensitivity or FDR improvement rather than runtime measurement — this skill only addresses wall-clock scaling, not rescoring performance gains. The data are DIA or spectral library generation jobs — the timing workflow targets data-driven rescoring of search engine results; job types 'CollisionEnergCalibration' and 'SpectralLibraryGeneration' follow different pipelines. Only a single small RAW file is processed — the ~4-fold multiprocessing speedup (~1 h vs ~15 min) was reported for 15 MS files and will not be reproducible on one file. http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Configure Oktoberfest rescoring runs to quantify and exploit multiprocessing speedup: run each HLA raw-file combination twice (numThreads = 1 vs multiprocessing enabled), record per-step and total wall-clock timings, and verify the reported ~4-fold speedup on multi-file workloads. proteomics/v1 10.1002/pmic.202300112
skills.summary: Configure Oktoberfest rescoring runs to quantify and exploit multiprocessing speedup: run each HLA raw-file combination twice (numThreads = 1 vs multiprocessing enabled), record per-step and total wall-clock timings, and verify the reported ~4-fold speedup on multi-file workloads.

skills.search_text: nsaf-normalization Use when spectral counts from a Morpheus search of high-resolution accurate-mass MS/MS data must be converted into length-normalized, label-free NSAF values, especially when peptides are shared across protein families or isoforms/proteoforms. The data were searched with a search engine other than the Morpheus Mass Spectrometry Search Engine — MSpC requires Morpheus output. Quantification requires MS1 peak alignment and re-extraction or isobaric-tag intensities — NSAF is a spectral-count method whose stated advantages are dynamic range and speed, not MS1- or reporter-ion-based quantification. Peptides are all uniquely mapped and protein-family/isoform resolution is not needed — only unique NSAF is informative and the distributed-counting machinery is unnecessary. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Computes Normalized Spectral Abundance Factor (NSAF) values from Morpheus peptide-MS/MS search output using Morpheus Spectral Counter (MSpC), including both distributed and unique NSAF so protein families and isoforms/proteoforms can be quantified, not just uniquely resolved proteins. proteomics/v1 10.1002/pmic.201500420
skills.summary: Computes Normalized Spectral Abundance Factor (NSAF) values from Morpheus peptide-MS/MS search output using Morpheus Spectral Counter (MSpC), including both distributed and unique NSAF so protein families and isoforms/proteoforms can be quantified, not just uniquely resolved proteins.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The data were searched with a search engine other than the Morpheus Mass Spectrometry Search Engine — MSpC requires Morpheus output. Quantification requires MS1 peak alignment and re-extraction or isobaric-tag intensities — NSAF is a spectral-count method whose stated advantages are dynamic range and speed, not MS1- or reporter-ion-based quantification. The goal is waveform accuracy or image quality (ADC bias from residual moments, intravoxel phase dispersion) rather than optimization speed — use a simulation-based skill instead. The optimization targets readout trajectories or slice-select gradient design, which the GrOpt toolbox has not been used to optimize. Very long waveform designs (e.g., multiecho turbo-spin echo) where the default choice of N and dt may need adjustment and the 1-40 ms benchmark range may not hold. http://edamontology.org/topic_3300 http://edamontology.org/topic_3444 Benchmark the wall-clock compute time of GrOpt numerical optimizations (ADMM-based gradient waveform design in C) by averaging repeated single-threaded calls per constraint configuration, to verify on-the-fly (1-40 ms) waveform generation. proteomics/v1 10.1002/mrm.28384
skills.summary: Benchmark the wall-clock compute time of GrOpt numerical optimizations (ADMM-based gradient waveform design in C) by averaging repeated single-threaded calls per constraint configuration, to verify on-the-fly (1-40 ms) waveform generation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is waveform accuracy or image quality (ADC bias from residual moments, intravoxel phase dispersion) rather than optimization speed — use a simulation-based skill instead. The optimization targets readout trajectories or slice-select gradient design, which the GrOpt toolbox has not been used to optimize. Very long waveform designs (e.g., multiecho turbo-spin echo) where the default choice of N and dt may need adjustment and the 1-40 ms benchmark range may not hold.

skills.description: Use when you need to quantify how quickly and with how much memory a Java parser reads X!Tandem XML output files at different scales (thousands to hundreds of thousands of quality spectra), and to compile the timing/RAM results into a metrics table.
skills.name: parsing-performance-metrics-tabulation
skills.search_text: parsing-performance-metrics-tabulation Use when you need to quantify how quickly and with how much memory a Java parser reads X!Tandem XML output files at different scales (thousands to hundreds of thousands of quality spectra), and to compile the timing/RAM results into a metrics table. Input results come from other search engines (e.g. MASCOT .dat files or OMSSA result files) — use Mascot-Dat File or OMSSA Parser instead, since XTandem Parser only extracts information from X!Tandem output xml files. The goal is visualization or biological analysis of identifications rather than parser performance benchmarking — the paper recommends PeptideShaker as a search engine independent platform for that purpose. You need to parse spectra itself rather than an X!Tandem search output; this skill only times reading of already-produced X!Tandem XML result files. http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Benchmarks the wall-clock parsing time and peak memory usage of XTandem Parser when reading X!Tandem XML result files of different sizes, reproducing the paper's Table 1 metrics (parsing time vs. number of quality spectra/valid models) and the <1 GB RAM constraint. proteomics/v1 10.1002/pmic.200900759
skills.summary: Benchmarks the wall-clock parsing time and peak memory usage of XTandem Parser when reading X!Tandem XML result files of different sizes, reproducing the paper's Table 1 metrics (parsing time vs. number of quality spectra/valid models) and the <1 GB RAM constraint.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input results come from other search engines (e.g. MASCOT .dat files or OMSSA result files) — use Mascot-Dat File or OMSSA Parser instead, since XTandem Parser only extracts information from X!Tandem output xml files. The goal is visualization or biological analysis of identifications rather than parser performance benchmarking — the paper recommends PeptideShaker as a search engine independent platform for that purpose. You need to parse spectra itself rather than an X!Tandem search output; this skill only times reading of already-produced X!Tandem XML result files.

skills.search_text: peak-array-decoding Use when mzIdentML-referenced peak list files (mzData, mzXML, mzML, MGF, DTA, MS2, PKL) must be parsed in Java to decode per-spectrum m/z-intensity peak arrays, scan/precursor metadata, and cvParam entries. The input is an mzIdentML file and spectra are expected from it — mzIdentML files do not contain spectra data but only refer to external peak list files, so decode peaks from the referenced file instead. A flat MGF file is all the downstream tool needs — jmzReader-gui can export all supported file formats directly into the commonly used mgf format, so no custom peak-array decoding code is required. The goal is archiving or submitting data to PRIDE / ProteomeXchange rather than extracting peaks for mzIdentML-based processing — this library parses peak lists, it does not handle archive submission. http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Decodes per-spectrum m/z-intensity peak arrays and their metadata (spectrum id/index, cvParams, scan number, MS level, precursor ion info) from XML-based MS peak list files such as mzData and mzXML using the jmzReader Java API, so spectra referenced by mzIdentML become reachable through one common interface. proteomics/v1 10.1002/pmic.201100578
skills.summary: Decodes per-spectrum m/z-intensity peak arrays and their metadata (spectrum id/index, cvParams, scan number, MS level, precursor ion info) from XML-based MS peak list files such as mzData and mzXML using the jmzReader Java API, so spectra referenced by mzIdentML become reachable through one common interface.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is an mzIdentML file and spectra are expected from it — mzIdentML files do not contain spectra data but only refer to external peak list files, so decode peaks from the referenced file instead. A flat MGF file is all the downstream tool needs — jmzReader-gui can export all supported file formats directly into the commonly used mgf format, so no custom peak-array decoding code is required. The goal is archiving or submitting data to PRIDE / ProteomeXchange rather than extracting peaks for mzIdentML-based processing — this library parses peak lists, it does not handle archive submission.

skills.name: peak-node-representation
skills.search_text: peak-node-representation Use when MS/MS peak lists (m/z and intensity per fragment peak) must be converted into a spectrum-graph (one node per peak, edges labeled with mass differences) before peptide identification or modification-tolerant matching, e.g. as input to Popitam. The input is already a spectrum graph or a scored peptide list — this skill only converts raw peak lists into graph form. The goal is full peptide identification/ranking by correlation score; this skill produces only the intermediate graph representation that Popitam parses, not the ranked peptides themselves. The data are MS1 profiles or non-tandem spectra — the representation is specific to MS/MS fragment peak data. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 Builds a structured spectrum-graph representation of a source MS/MS spectrum, where each fragment peak becomes a node carrying its mass (m/z) and intensity, and directed edges between nodes are annotated with mass differences. The analysis goal is Tm estimation or MC normalization rather than quantifying how smoothing perturbs the curve shape Input data are not DSF melting curves from the SimpleDSFviewer exemplar or an equivalent raw/smoothed MC pair on a shared temperature axis Only one curve (raw or smoothed) is available — a paired raw-minus-smoothed difference cannot be computed http://edamontology.org/topic_3318 Quantifies how much SimpleDSFviewer's built-in MC smoothing alters differential scanning fluorimetry melting curves by computing per-point raw-minus-smoothed differences, then recovering regional maxima in the folded (flat) and denatured (high-peak) areas of the Figure 4c surface plot (0.0392 vs 2.517). proteomics/v1 10.1002/pro.3703
